articles.title: Media suggests what CIA chief discussed during Moscow visit
articles.body:
CIA chief proposed trilateral talks during Moscow visit – Axios
CIA Director John Ratcliffe proposed a trilateral meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump and Vladimir Zelensky during his covert trip to Moscow in an effort to find a resolution to the ongoing Ukraine conflict, Axios has reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.
Ratcliffe made an unannounced trip to Moscow on August 25. The following day, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed that contact between the two countries’ intelligence services had taken place, but said Putin had not met with the CIA chief. “Of course, President Putin is immediately briefed on everything,” Peskov said, calling the meeting “a positive phenomenon” while declining to give further details.
Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) chief Sergei Naryshkin later confirmed that he had met with Ratcliffe in Moscow. Naryshkin said the issues discussed were related to the intelligence services. Axios reported that Ratcliffe also met with Federal Security Service (FSB) Director Alexander Bortnikov.
US officials briefed Zelensky on the Moscow talks and the plan for a trilateral summit. They also said Ratcliffe had discussed the possibility of restarting peace talks, the outlet reported.
Earlier last week, Trump described the visit as “semi-routine.” When asked by talk show host Glenn Beck whether Putin planned on “testing NATO resolve,” or whether Ratcliffe discussed US sanctions on Iran, Trump replied “none of the above.”
Ratcliffe’s visit was the first known trip to Moscow by a CIA director since William Burns traveled there in November 2021. The last known face-to-face meeting between the CIA and SVR chiefs was in Ankara in November 2022, when Burns met Naryshkin to discuss nuclear escalation risks and detained US citizens.
The last publicly disclosed contact between Ratcliffe and a senior Russian official was a March 2025 phone call with SVR chief Sergey Naryshkin. The two sides agreed to maintain dialogue to “promote international stability and security” and reduce tensions between Moscow and Washington, the SVR said.

articles.title: ‘It makes no sense’ for Moscow to attack NATO – Finland’s president
articles.body:
‘It makes no sense’ for Moscow to attack NATO – Finland’s president
Finnish President Alexander Stubb has said that he doesn’t believe speculations that Russia is planning to attack NATO countries.
Russia has repeatedly rejected claims that it has aggressive designs against the bloc, saying that they are only made by Western politicians to distract the public from problems at home and justify growing military spending.
During his interview with the German tabloid Bild on Saturday, Stubb was asked to weigh in on the assessment by the Defense Ministry in Berlin that Russia could invade NATO territory by 2029.
“If someone had such a crystal ball – wonderful. But I just don’t see any evidence or facts for it,” he replied.
“First, I have intelligence findings. And secondly, we have a deterrence – and this deterrence is stronger than that of any other military power anywhere in the world,” the Finnish president added.
Given NATO’s conventional forces, missile arsenals and nuclear weapons stockpiles, “it does not make sense for any power in the world to test the resolve of this alliance,” he said.
According to Stubb, Russia is also preoccupied with the Ukraine conflict.
“I simply don’t see that they could now suddenly mobilize forces for two fronts,” he noted.
“I’m not saying: ‘Relax.’ You should always prepare for the worst to prevent it,” the Finnish president said.
He accused Moscow of waging “information warfare” against the West, saying that “Russia wants us Europeans to sit here and discuss: Will Russia escalate?.. Will Russia attack NATO and Europe?”
Stubb again urged NATO to continue its support for Kiev amid the ongoing conflict with Moscow. Finland joined the bloc in 2023, abandoning its longstanding policy of neutrality.
“We have to understand, you in Germany and we in Finland, that Ukraine is the best security guarantee we have against Russia. If Ukraine loses, we lose,” he argued.
Moscow maintains that a conflict with NATO is only possible if the bloc launches an aggression against Russia first.
Earlier this week, Moscow told the UK that its military facilities and equipment in Ukraine and beyond could become legitimate targets for Russia if Kiev continues to use British-supplied weapons for strikes on Russian territory.
Russian officials also previously warned that if Latvia, Estonia, and Lithuania knowingly help to facilitate Ukrainian drone attacks against northwestern Russia, Moscow could consider them complicit in those actions and would have the right to self-defense under the UN Charter.

articles.title: Finland says it ‘makes no sense’ for Russia to risk attack on a Nato nation
articles.body:
Finland says it ‘makes no sense’ for Russia to risk attack on a Nato nation
President Stubb said he did not believe Moscow was in a position to go to war with the military alliance
Finland’s President Alexander Stubb said he did not believe Russia would risk an attack against a Nato country, telling Germany’s Bild newspaper it would “make no sense” to test the resolve of the alliance.
Western officials have warned of a growing risk of Russian hybrid operations, including cyberattacks, against European countries potentially leading to a direct confrontation with the Nato alliance. German officials have said they assess Russia would be in a position to attack a Nato country by 2029.
“If anyone has a crystal ball like that – that’s great. I simply see neither evidence nor facts to support it,” he told Bild in an interview published on Saturday, adding he did not believe that Russia “would ever want to attack Nato, the world’s most powerful military alliance”.
Stubb, whose country joined Nato in 2023, abandoning its previous policy of neutrality following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine a year earlier, said the alliance had to be prepared for any scenario but he did not believe Moscow was in a position to go to war with Nato.
He said Nato’s strength in conventional weapons, missiles and nuclear weapons was too strong to attack, adding that he had intelligence information to back his assessment.

articles.title: Russia threatens mass strikes on Ukraine energy sites as Kyiv depot death toll hits 38
articles.body:
As Moscow warns of a fresh bombing campaign and Kyiv absorbs one of the deadliest strikes to hit its own soil since the invasion began, four years of fighting show no sign of nearing a diplomatic end.
Russia's defence ministry says it is preparing large-scale strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, framing the move as retaliation for Kyiv's attacks on Russian territory, as the death toll from a Russian strike on an ammunition depot near the Ukrainian capital climbed to 38.
"The Russian Armed Forces have begun preparations for massive strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in response to what Moscow describes as ongoing attacks by the Kyiv regime on Russia’s civilian infrastructure and fuel and energy facilities," the defence ministry in Moscow said on Telegram.
The warning revives fears of a repeat of last winter, when Moscow's bombardment of Ukrainian power plants devastated the country's grid and left millions without heat or electricity in sub-zero temperatures.
Both sides have escalated long-range strikes over the past several months, hitting warehouses, refineries, ports and ships, with rising civilian casualties.
Depot strike toll climbs to 38
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sunday that the death toll from Saturday's Russian drone strike on a munitions depot in the village of Myla, in the Bucha district near Kyiv, had risen to 38, with 20 people injured and four still missing. Writing on Telegram, Zelensky said "the extent of contamination in the area is significant" as emergency crews worked to extinguish the remaining fires and bomb disposal teams cleared the site.
The strike triggered a massive detonation and secondary explosions that sent flames into surrounding residential areas, damaging around 50 buildings and forcing the evacuation of more than 380 residents, according to regional officials. Among the dead was Taras Didych, mayor of the nearby village of Dmytrivka. It is one of the deadliest single incidents Kyiv's suburbs have seen since Russia's full-scale invasion began more than four years ago.
Ukrainian prosecutors have opened a criminal negligence investigation focused on why explosives were being stored so close to homes.
A third day of sustained attacks
The Myla strike capped a third consecutive day of Russian aerial bombardment — among the most sustained since spring.
Russia's military said it also struck a cement and asbestos plant in Kyiv on Sunday, alleging its warehouses were being used to store explosives, along with a drone and munitions manufacturing site.
Overall, Russia launched two Iskander-M ballistic missiles and 130 drones of various types between late Saturday and early Sunday, the Ukrainian air force said.
Ukraine, for its part, struck an oil refinery in northwestern Russia with drones, sparking a fire, according to local Russian authorities.
The Kirishi oil refinery in Russia’s Leningrad region is the country's second-largest production plant, with the capacity to process around 20 million tonnes of crude oil a year for jet fuel and diesel.
Kyiv has increasingly targeted Russia's energy and oil infrastructure — refineries, pumping stations and storage depots — as part of a strategy officials say is meant to pressure Moscow economically toward ending the war.

articles.title: Iran's Khamenei calls for Muslim unity against Israel, US
articles.body:
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of events across the Middle East.
Here are the key developments on Sunday morning:
• Israel has launched fresh attacks in Gaza, killing at least one person and injuring several others in a strike in Deir al-Balah. The Israeli military claimed it killed a Hamas commander in yesterday's attack in Jabalia refugee camp.
• Fresh Israeli attacks have been reported in southern Lebanon in violation of the fragile ceasefire deal.
• Extremist settlers are continuing to rampage in the West Bank as pogroms against Palestinians intensify across the occupied territory. Attacks against Palestinian civilians have been reported in a dozen locations, including villages near Nablus and Ramallah, Masafer Yatta and Al-Mughayyir.
• On Saturday, settlers attacked an American news crew near the besieged village of Qusra, drawing a rare condemnation from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. In Masafer Yatta, settlers kidnapped British activist Finn Joughin, whose whereabouts remain unknown.
Assad-era Syrian commander killed in Tartus security raid
Firas Abdul Karim Hammoud, known as "al-Khal", was the former commander of special forces in the unit once known as the 25th Division, the Syrian Interior Ministry said in a statement.
The ministry said Internal Security forces raided Hammoud’s hideout in the town of Safita in Tartus province after tracking his movements across several areas.
The Palestinian Foreign Ministry has strongly condemned the escalating attacks of the Israeli army and illegal settlers in the West Bank town of Al-Mughayyir, calling for international intervention to end the violence after officials warned of a 20-day "suffocating siege".
The town, northeast of Ramallah, has had its entrance gates sealed, with residents reportedly permitted to move in and out for only two hours each day. The ministry said the restrictions were aimed at isolating the community and displacing its population.
In a statement, the ministry said Israeli measures also included preventing ambulances from entering the town amid what it described as the indiscriminate targeting of residents.
Two civilians were killed near the Druze-majority city of Sweida in southern Syria on Sunday, two local security sources told AFP, during suspected clashes between local armed groups and government forces.
The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights monitor reported the same death toll, adding that government forces and armed groups from the Druze minority group had been exchanging fire since Saturday night.
Tensions have been high in Sweida province since clashes between Druze and government-aligned forces last year led to some of the worst communal violence since the fall of longtime Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad in 2024.
A Druze security source told AFP on condition of anonymity that a shell launched from a government-controlled area "targeted the outskirts of the city of Sweida, striking a tractor and killing two people on board, the driver and a woman who was with him".
Sweida city and other parts of the surrounding Druze-majority province are run by armed groups and are the last major areas outside the grasp of Syria's new Islamist authorities, who have been trying to unite the country after toppling Assad.
Tanker struck by projectile in Strait of Hormuz: UKMTO
A tanker was struck by an unknown projectile while transiting inbound through the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said on Sunday.
The incident occurred 12 nautical miles north of Oman's Khasab, UKMTO said in an advisory note, adding that no casualties or environmental impact were reported.
UAE, Egypt central banks coordinating on US sanctions
The United Arab Emirates and Egyptian central banks are coordinating on Banque Misr, they said on Sunday, after the US imposed sanctions on the bank's UAE branches over its alleged dealings with Iran.
The US Treasury on Friday said it was cutting off the bank's UAE operations from dollar transactions after accusing it of ties with Iran.
Banque Misr will take all necessary measures to conduct its business as usual, the central banks said in their joint statement.
US military chiefs warn Hegseth on Iran war: report
US military officials have warned Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that a prolonged war against Iran is unsustainable and jeopardising the military’s ability to respond to other threats around the world, the Washington Post has reported, citing anonymous sources.
In a 14 August report, army, navy and air force chiefs told Hegseth that the war has been "too much for too long" and is putting military readiness under strain.
Israeli forces have raided Qalandia refugee camp north of Jerusalem and the UNRWA-run Qalandia vocational training centre in East Jerusalem for the second time in a week, according to Palestinian news agency WAFA.
Security forces seized the UN-run centre on Tuesday and expelled dozens of staff, drawing international condemnation.
Israeli forces seize UNRWA's Qalandiya Training Centre on 26 August 2026. [Getty]
Israel says Hamas commander killed in Deir al-Balah strike
Iraq sentenced a US-sanctioned oil official to seven years in prison after he was arrested as part of a government-led anti-corruption campaign, the country's anti-graft body said on Sunday.
Deputy oil minister for distribution affairs Ali al-Bahadli is among dozens of officials who were detained in June during anti-graft raids that took place in several areas, mostly in Baghdad's fortified Green Zone.
The Commission of Integrity said in a statement that an anti-corruption court sentenced Bahadli to seven years in prison for "illicit gains".
The ruling requires Bahadli to return to the state an amount equivalent to more than $20 million in ill-gotten gains, in addition to paying a fine of the same amount.
The United States imposed sanctions on Bahadli in May, accusing him of fraudulently mixing Iraqi and Iranian oil as part of a scheme to help Iran avoid sanctions.
Turkey, Saudi, Pakistan to hold first defence pact meeting
Turkey will host Saudi Arabia and Pakistan for the first ministerial meeting of their new regional defence grouping on Monday, Turkish sources said Sunday.
The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed earlier this month commits the three countries to mutual defence in the event of any of them being attacked.
The pact came against a backdrop of war between the United States and Iran and attacks in the region from Tehran-backed Houthi rebels.
The meeting in Istanbul will set up a "political and defence strategic committee" involving foreign and defence ministers and military chiefs, Turkish foreign ministry sources said.
The agreement unites NATO's second-largest army, Turkey, with the Islamic world's only nuclear-armed state, Pakistan, and the leading Gulf power in Saudi Arabia.
Monday's meeting will be chaired by the Turkish foreign and defence ministers as well as the chief of the general staff.
Pakistan is sending Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, along with the defence minister and the commander of the defence forces.
Saudi Arabia will be represented by its foreign minister, the defence minister and the chief of the general staff, Turkish sources said.
As well as international security, the participants plan to address boosting defence capabilities, the interoperability of their armed forces, and their cooperation in the defence industry, Ankara said.
Israel has killed at least five Palestinians in Gaza over the past 24 hours, according to Gaza's health ministry.
At least 1,318 people have been killed by Israeli forces since the "ceasefire" was supposed to come into effect in October, the ministry said in its daily bulletin.
The Israeli army has carried out a "massive" explosion in the border town of Houla in Lebanon's Marjayoun district, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency.
At least one killed in Israeli drone strike in Gaza
At least one Palestinian was killed and several others, including a child, were injured on Sunday in an Israeli drone strike in Deir al-Balah, central gaza, according to Palestinian news agency WAFA, citing medical sources.
The strike reportedly targeted a group of Palestinians near Akila Street.
Israel's Ben-Gvir boasts of worse prison conditions
Israel's far-right national security minister on Sunday boasted of worsening conditions for Palestinian prisoners as he visited female inmates.
Two months before elections, Itamar Ben-Gvir posted a video in which a veiled woman, her face blurred out, said that prisoners had "extremely bad" conditions and "don't get any rights, and we have particular needs as women".
"We haven't bathed for three days and we haven't changed our underwear," she said, warning of the risk of disease.
Ben-Gvir responds approvingly as he compares the treatment to that of captives held for up to two years by Hamas and other fighters in Gaza following the 7 October 2023 attack.
"Our hostages had no shampoo and had no such conditions. I am proud that we have succeeded in reducing the terrorists' prison conditions to the bare minimum. The summer camps in the prisons are over," Ben Gvir said.
Militant settlers are continuing to rampage in the occupied West Bank as pogroms against Palestinians intensify across the territory. Attacks against Palestinian civilians were reported in a dozen locations on Sunday, including in villages near Nablus and Ramallah, Masafer Yatta and Al-Mughayyir.
Hundreds of settlers raided Islamic religious sites in the village of Awarta, southeast of Nablus, under the protection of Israeli forces.
Meanwhile, Israeli soldiers began destroying Palestinian-owned land in the town of Deir Ballut, in the central West Bank.
Settlers besiege Palestinians in Qusra, a village near Nablus, 29 August 2026. [Getty]
Israel claims killed Hamas commander in Gaza strike
Iran supreme leader calls for unity among Muslim countries
Iran's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei on Sunday called on Muslim countries in the region to unite against the United States and Israel, in a written message issued six months on from the start of the Middle East war.
Khamenei, in power since shortly after his father Ali Khamenei was killed at the start of the war on February 28, has yet to be seen in public since his appointment, and authorities have not released any video or audio of him.
"The solution to the problems of the Islamic nations is unity of words, friendship, and cooperation on the path of goodness," he said Sunday as Shia Muslims marked the birthday of the Prophet Mohammed.
"Anyone, in any position, who does anything that leads to division among Muslims and creates conflict in the Muslim community, knowingly or unknowingly, intentionally or unintentionally, has served the purpose of the enemies of Islam," he added, according to his official website.
The supreme leader called on the rulers of regional countries to "recognise your real enemy, understand its plan, and confront it", referring to the US and Israel.
Iran's ties with its neighbours have soured after it targeted US military bases and civilian infrastructure across the region, including in Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain.

Turkey, Saudi, Pakistan to hold first defence pact meeting
Turkey will host Saudi Arabia and Pakistan for the first ministerial meeting of their new regional defence grouping on Monday, Turkish sources said Sunday.
The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed earlier this month commits the three countries to mutual defence in the event of any of them being attacked.
The pact came against a backdrop of war between the United States and Iran and attacks in the region from Tehran-backed Houthi rebels.
The meeting in Istanbul will set up a "political and defence strategic committee" involving foreign and defence ministers and military chiefs, Turkish foreign ministry sources said.
The agreement unites NATO's second-largest army, Turkey, with the Islamic world's only nuclear-armed state, Pakistan, and the leading Gulf power in Saudi Arabia.
Monday's meeting will be chaired by the Turkish foreign and defence ministers as well as the chief of the general staff.
Pakistan is sending Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, along with the defence minister and the commander of the defence forces.
Saudi Arabia will be represented by its foreign minister, the defence minister and the chief of the general staff, Turkish sources said.
As well as international security, the participants plan to address boosting defence capabilities, the interoperability of their armed forces, and their cooperation in the defence industry, Ankara said.
Israel has killed at least five Palestinians in Gaza over the past 24 hours, according to Gaza's health ministry.
At least 1,318 people have been killed by Israeli forces since the "ceasefire" was supposed to come into effect in October, the ministry said in its daily bulletin.
The Israeli army has carried out a "massive" explosion in the border town of Houla in Lebanon's Marjayoun district, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency.
At least one killed in Israeli drone strike in Gaza
At least one Palestinian was killed and several others, including a child, were injured on Sunday in an Israeli drone strike in Deir al-Balah, central gaza, according to Palestinian news agency WAFA, citing medical sources.
The strike reportedly targeted a group of Palestinians near Akila Street.
Israel's Ben-Gvir boasts of worse prison conditions
Israel's far-right national security minister on Sunday boasted of worsening conditions for Palestinian prisoners as he visited female inmates.
Two months before elections, Itamar Ben-Gvir posted a video in which a veiled woman, her face blurred out, said that prisoners had "extremely bad" conditions and "don't get any rights, and we have particular needs as women".
"We haven't bathed for three days and we haven't changed our underwear," she said, warning of the risk of disease.
Ben-Gvir responds approvingly as he compares the treatment to that of captives held for up to two years by Hamas and other fighters in Gaza following the 7 October 2023 attack.
"Our hostages had no shampoo and had no such conditions. I am proud that we have succeeded in reducing the terrorists' prison conditions to the bare minimum. The summer camps in the prisons are over," Ben Gvir said.
Militant settlers are continuing to rampage in the occupied West Bank as pogroms against Palestinians intensify across the territory. Attacks against Palestinian civilians were reported in a dozen locations on Sunday, including in villages near Nablus and Ramallah, Masafer Yatta and Al-Mughayyir.
Hundreds of settlers raided Islamic religious sites in the village of Awarta, southeast of Nablus, under the protection of Israeli forces.
Meanwhile, Israeli soldiers began destroying Palestinian-owned land in the town of Deir Ballut, in the central West Bank.
Settlers besiege Palestinians in Qusra, a village near Nablus, 29 August 2026. [Getty]

Iran supreme leader calls for unity among Muslim countries
Iran's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei on Sunday called on Muslim countries in the region to unite against the United States and Israel, in a written message issued six months on from the start of the Middle East war.
Khamenei, in power since shortly after his father Ali Khamenei was killed at the start of the war on February 28, has yet to be seen in public since his appointment, and authorities have not released any video or audio of him.
"The solution to the problems of the Islamic nations is unity of words, friendship, and cooperation on the path of goodness," he said Sunday as Shia Muslims marked the birthday of the Prophet Mohammed.
"Anyone, in any position, who does anything that leads to division among Muslims and creates conflict in the Muslim community, knowingly or unknowingly, intentionally or unintentionally, has served the purpose of the enemies of Islam," he added, according to his official website.
The supreme leader called on the rulers of regional countries to "recognise your real enemy, understand its plan, and confront it", referring to the US and Israel.
Iran's ties with its neighbours have soured after it targeted US military bases and civilian infrastructure across the region, including in Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain.

articles.title: Kyiv seeks answers over 38 deaths in Russian strike on arms depot
articles.body:
The death toll from a Russian strike on an ammunition depot in Ukraine's Kyiv region has risen to 38, with four people still missing, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday.
The deadliest Russian strike in the Kyiv area this year took place late Friday as Moscow launched an intense campaign of attacks on the Ukrainian capital, which has continued over the weekend.
Friday's blast hit a military facility that held artillery shells, mines, drones and other ammunition.
Zelenskyy said on Telegram that first responders had managed to extinguish most of the fires. However, the scale of contamination in the area was significant and this work would continue for as long as necessary.
The president released video footage showing firefighting teams battling blazes and removing debris from destroyed buildings.
In its intensified attacks on the country, Russia over the last week launched nearly 2,000 strike drones, more than 1,600 aerial bombs, and 31 missiles, including North Korean ballistic missiles, Zelenskyy said.
"We are seeking just responses to every Russian strike and crime. They will certainly come," he said.
Overnight Saturday, plumes of black smoke poured over the capital's western suburbs, while videos published by Ukraine's rescue services showed homes near the blast epicenter in flames, reported Agence France-Presse (AFP).
The attack was the second to hit a munitions depot near Kyiv in less than two months, with officials expressing anger that arms were still being stored so close to residential areas.
Both Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes on each other in recent months, pushing civilian casualties to their highest level since Moscow invaded in 2022.
"Those who allowed this to happen must be held accountable for their decisions ... ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas," President Zelenskyy said in a post on X.
The blast forced hundreds to evacuate and damaged multiple homes, including a care facility for elderly and disabled people, he added.
The mayor of the nearby town of Dmytrivka were also among the dead, Kyiv region Gov. Tymur Tkachenko said on Telegram.
Residents in the area told AFP the explosion was "terrifying."
"We thought we were being bombed. No one knew it was a detonation," said Yana Doneli, resident of a nearby town.
Zelenskyy blamed the incident on "horrific negligence," saying ammunition should not have been stored there.
Ukrainian prosecutors said they had opened an investigation into criminal negligence.
"On Aug. 28 at around 8:10 p.m. (1710 GMT), an unmanned aerial vehicle ... fell on or struck the grounds of an enterprise in the town of Myla," the office of Ukraine's prosecutor general said.
Myla is a small town on the outskirts of western Kyiv.
"A large-scale fire broke out on the enterprise's grounds and detonation began," prosecutors added.
The prosecutor's office said that its investigation would focus on "the legality of the ... storage of explosive objects and materials on the enterprise's grounds," as well as whether the owner, whom it did not name, had the "necessary permits and approvals."
Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky expressed regret that a "lesson" had not been learned following a previous deadly strike on a munitions depot near Kyiv in July.
That investigation revealed serious failings on the part of a state-owned company, which did not comply with regulations regarding the proximity of residential buildings.
"In the fifth year of the full-scale invasion, making the same mistakes over and over is criminal negligence," he said on Telegram.
"Everyone responsible, without exception, must face severe punishment so that such situations never happen again," said Koretsky.

articles.title: America lost its longest war five years ago. This is what victory looks like for the Taliban
articles.body:
America lost its longest war five years ago. This is what victory looks like for the Taliban
“When Ashraf Ghani goes, we’ll go with him. And he’ll go when the Americans do.”
The conversation took place on the balcony of a luxury high-rise in Shahr-e Naw, central Kabul. The man speaking to me was a young government employee, and Ashraf Ghani was serving his second term as president of the Islamic Republic of Afghanistan. It was May 2017. The republic had four years and three months left.
A city living on borrowed time
Afghanistan at the time could best be described with a line from Dickens: “It was the best of times, it was the worst of times… we had everything before us, we had nothing before us.” Kabul was both deeply Westernized and full of contradictions. The former was fueled by the abundance of foreigners and foreign aid; the latter by the unending fighting and terrorist attacks.
Downtown, you could find nightclubs throwing Valentine’s Day and Halloween parties, modeling agencies, coffee shops serving cheesecake, bowling alleys, and tattoo parlors. On the outskirts, tent camps were expanding to accommodate internally displaced people – refugees from the provinces, mostly in the south, whose homes had been destroyed by the war. Street boys begged in English: “Give me one hundred dollars!” Artists painted murals warning about domestic violence, fashionable women wore jeans and bright makeup, and Western NGOs taught Afghan children to skateboard.
At the same time, some places – including the park in Shahr-e Naw itself – were unsafe even in broad daylight because of the number of drug addicts, while robberies and kidnappings had become routine. After sunset, the city shut down. Several years later, The New York Times would call Kabul a city of hope and despair – an apt metaphor.
To protect itself from the constant bombings, Kabul grew a shell of concrete walls and checkpoints. There seemed to be as many police officers and soldiers on the streets as civilians, while American surveillance balloons hovered continuously over the city. None of it helped much. That same May, while I was there, a tanker truck packed with explosives detonated in the diplomatic quarter, killing more than 90 people and wounding around 400. Smaller incidents had long since ceased to qualify as news. One of my editors gave me a simple rule:
“If there’s a terrorist attack in Kabul and fewer than ten people are killed, don’t write about it. That’s not news.”
Politics and public life were no less remarkable. Afghanistan’s parliament had as many women as the US Congress, yet in the center of the capital a mob lynched Farkhunda Malikzada, a young Afghan woman, after a mullah falsely accused her of burning the Quran. Corruption broke every record, and the central government was weak. Hamid Karzai, the republic’s first president, had been dubbed the “president of Kabul.” Ashraf Ghani was already merely the “president of the presidential palace.” A provincial governor removed from office could simply declare that the president had no authority over him and remain at his post. Drug production reached unprecedented levels: according to the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, 84% of the opiates on the global market in 2017 originated in Afghanistan.
This was what years of NATO’s military presence had made of the country and its capital. Once the troops withdrew, the existing order was bound to collapse.
The war that kept changing uniforms
The arrival of the United States and its allies in Afghanistan opened a new chapter in a civil war that, with varying degrees of intensity, had already been raging for 23 years.
Pandora’s box was opened in 1978, when the left came to power. The United States, Pakistan, China, and the Gulf states began actively arming the opposition, while the new government asked the Soviet Union for help. From 1979 to 1989, the Limited Contingent of Soviet Forces carried out what Moscow called its “internationalist duty” in Afghanistan, supporting a friendly government and controlling the major cities and some of the roads – the most any foreign army could hope to hold in the country’s mountainous terrain.
After the Soviet withdrawal, Mohammad Najibullah’s pro-Soviet government survived for roughly four years before being overthrown by the mujahideen: warlords who had first fought the shuravi – “Soviets” in Dari – and then turned their guns on one another in a struggle for power. The Taliban entered Kabul in 1996, bringing down the mujahideen government everywhere except the Panjshir Valley. The international community then forgot about Afghanistan for five years. It remembered the country only after the September 11, 2001 attacks, because Osama bin Laden was hiding there.
Immediately after the attacks came an episode recounted in ethnography classes to every student specializing in Afghanistan. George W. Bush issued the Taliban an ultimatum: hand over bin Laden. They refused. The official explanation was that there was no evidence linking him to the attacks. But there was an unofficial reason as well: bin Laden was a guest in Afghanistan. For the Pashtuns – the country’s largest ethnic group, to which the Taliban also belong – the rules of hospitality are sacred, and surrendering a guest to his enemy would bring shame for generations.
Uninterested in the finer points of the local mindset, Bush spent a month bombing Afghanistan and destroying the Taliban’s air force and air defenses. Then came the ground operation, first carried out with the help of allied forces – the same mujahideen – and later by US Marines under Operation Enduring Freedom. The United States had entered the longest war in its history and, at the same time, decided to build a democracy in Afghanistan – a bold idea for a country still living, in many respects, in the Middle Ages, with only a third of its population able to read and write. American filmmakers would later explore the absurdity of the situation and Washington’s profound failure to understand the country in War Machine, starring Brad Pitt.
For the first several years, things went reasonably well. Hamid Karzai, mentioned above, was elected president, a parliament was elected, and the United Nations and other international organizations threw themselves into reconstruction. While much of the money ended up in officials’ pockets, life did improve in some respects: child mortality declined, and the number of young women attending universities rose.
By 2005, however, the Taliban had recovered from their defeat and launched a guerrilla war in the south, where they found no shortage of supporters. Again, I think back to those university ethnography classes. We were taught that Afghans prefer something of their own, even if it is bad, to something good imposed by outsiders. In other words, Afghans have always hated occupiers. NATO troops – who periodically stormed into the women’s quarters of homes during raids or killed civilians, whether by mistake or out of fear – were no exception. The Taliban, for all their conservatism and radical methods, were still their own. Their values did not clash with those of Afghanistan’s rural heartland. I still remember how Taliban fighters were welcomed in Kabul during a three-day ceasefire in 2018: people gave them flowers, took selfies with them, brought them food, hugged them, and wept.
During the years of the American presence, much of the resentment toward the Soviet Union had faded.
”Yes, you fought us, but you fought well, like men,” former mujahideen told me again and again in different parts of the country. “You were brave: face to face, and the stronger man won. But these people? They bomb us from airplanes.”
The runway at the end of the world
On August 15, 2021, a message from Kabul woke me. It was from an Afghan journalist I knew.
”They’re here.”
“Who?”
“The Taliban. They’ve taken the city. It’s over.”
I had flown out of Kabul in February, and that assignment had been my bleakest: three or four explosions a day, activists and politicians being assassinated, Taliban patrols operating barely 12 miles from the capital. Kabul was practically under siege. Intense localized fighting raged in the south, official figures put the death toll at a hundred people a day, and provincial capitals kept changing hands.
Biden had announced that American troops would leave Afghanistan by September 11 – the irony was hard to miss – but analysts remained fairly optimistic. After all, Najibullah had held on for several years. Why couldn’t Ghani? Operation Enduring Freedom had long since been replaced by the noncombat Resolute Support mission, with alliance troops training and advising their Afghan counterparts so they could stand up to the Taliban on their own. Depending on the forecast, the republic was expected to survive anywhere from two to six months.
The Afghan armed forces did, in fact, have plenty of combat-ready units: Special Forces and commando brigades, as well as the Grom and Gardez regional army corps based in Khost and Kandahar. But every conversation I had with the military left me with the same heavy feeling. Many complained that both their allies and their commanders were indifferent to their fate, while morale in more remote areas was catastrophically low. The commander of a checkpoint in Kunar Province told me he had gone several months without food, ammunition, or pay. Of the eight soldiers under his command, three were suffering from depression. One no longer got out of bed and was preparing to die, even though his wound was not serious; he was also using drugs. Two others were planning to defect to the Taliban. Every evening, the militants used loudspeakers to urge them to surrender, promising to spare their lives – a common practice at the time, and the Taliban generally kept their word. The commander himself, though “tired to death,” as he put it, had no intention of giving up. He had killed too many of them to expect mercy.
”No one will fight for the president. Nobody likes him,” he told me as we said goodbye. “And the president wouldn’t fight for us, either. The Americans deceived him, and he’ll deceive us.”
His words about the president proved prophetic: Ashraf Ghani fled to Uzbekistan before Kabul had even fallen fully under Taliban control. But the checkpoint commander was wrong about his own future. He survived the fall of the government and became a taxi driver. Tens of thousands of his former comrades found work as security guards, construction workers, shopkeepers, or day laborers. The new government granted them amnesty but did not trust them enough to keep them in the army.
But back to the morning of August 15. Mass panic gripped Kabul. A crowd rushed to the airport – the only place still under coalition control – tore down the barriers, and flooded the tarmac. Terrified people tried to force their way onto American planes, and their fear was entirely understandable: many remembered the public executions and ethnic cleansing of the Taliban’s first period in power. Photographs from Kabul in August 2021 bore an uncanny resemblance to those from Saigon in April 1975, when the Americans were also evacuating their allies. History does, after all, have a way of moving in circles. Kabul itself, incidentally, fell without a fight. Among those who spent weeks waiting for a flight and sleeping on the runways were many former members of the security forces who had gone home without firing a shot and hidden their uniforms.
”American troops cannot and should not be fighting in a war and dying in a war that Afghan forces are not willing to fight for themselves,” US President Joe Biden said in summing up the debacle.
”We were betrayed,” General Sami Sadat, a deputy commander of the Afghan army, told The New York Times.
Analysts now expected mass reprisals and another round of civil war. But Afghanistan – now the Islamic Emirate – was quiet.
A different kind of silence
A teapot filled with green tea sits on the desk of a Taliban official at the Ministry of Information. My hospitable host diligently keeps my cup full, pushes a dish of chewy candies toward me, and asks what I think of the new government. A month and a half has passed since the fall of the republic – or the “victory,” as the Taliban themselves call it.
”Have you been to our country before?”
“Yes.”
“And when was it better – then or now?”
“It’s much safer now,” I say. It is clearly the answer he expects, and one I can give with a clear conscience.
This time I arrived in Kabul from the north, after a 12-hour drive from Mazar-i-Sharif through the Salang Pass. Under the republic, such a journey would have been unthinkable. Fighting had raged all along the road. The reminders were everywhere: burned-out army vehicles stacked in pyramids, the walls of homes blown away by explosions, and the road itself, pocked with craters from mines and shelling. You can now walk at night in any part of Kabul, though few Afghans take advantage of the opportunity. No one yet understands what to expect from the new rulers. People fear them, despite all the leaders’ talk of peace and brotherhood. Yet after events that many Afghans experienced as the end of the world, life slipped back into its familiar rhythms with surprising speed. Government offices and banks were operating, stores were open, and there were no fewer women on the streets – and not all of them were wrapped in the famous blue burqas. The worst fears had not come true, at least not at that point.
”Just give us time,” the Taliban official says with a smile. “After the revolution, the Bolsheviks needed time to accomplish something, too.” He calls them “the Communists.” “Come back in five years, and everything will be different.”
And now, almost five years later, I do see Afghanistan again.
It is still quiet here, despite the conflict with Pakistan and divisions within the leadership. But it is a different kind of quiet.
The Emirate has many enemies, and its security services are exceptionally vigilant. To the Taliban, every foreigner is a potential spy. Tourists, reporters, and the staff of the humanitarian missions still operating in the country are kept under constant surveillance, while Afghans who speak with them can face trouble, up to and including arrest. The religious police, meanwhile, enforce compliance with Sharia. The sticks in the officers’ hands may be mostly for show, but people still try not to attract their attention.
Music is banned. There are many prohibitions, and a good number of them concern perfectly innocent things such as chess, which is now considered a form of gambling. The craters left by explosions have long since been patched. Restaurants that look far more like Dubai than Kabul are opening in Shahr-e Naw. The drug addicts were forcibly removed from the park long ago and sent to treatment centers that have almost no medicine. Girls still have not returned to school since the takeover, and working women are almost nowhere to be seen. No, unlike the republic, the Islamic Emirate is not a place of contradictions, and Kabul stopped being a city of despair long ago. But there is little hope left in it, either.
Downtown, the concrete walls are being dismantled. They are no longer needed now that the bombings have stopped. The republic-era murals have faded so badly that the words “We Want Peace” are barely legible. And Afghanistan has, indeed, enjoyed its longest stretch of peace in 40 years.

The President of Finland does not believe in Russia's attack on NATO and rules out a nuclear strike on Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Alexander Stubb said that he sees no evidence of Russia preparing to attack NATO. He also doubts that there will be a nuclear strike on Ukraine.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb said he sees no evidence of a possible Russian attack on NATO, and also expressed doubt that Moscow would use nuclear weapons against Ukraine. BILD reports, writes UNN.
I do not believe that Russia will ever want to attack the world's most powerful military alliance — NATO
He commented on Germany's warning that Russia could be capable of attacking NATO territory by 2029, noting that he sees "neither evidence nor facts" supporting such a scenario.

There is no point for any power in the world to test the resolve of this alliance
The President of Finland also expressed doubt about the possibility of a Russian nuclear strike on Ukraine. According to him, he raised the issue during a conversation with China's foreign minister, who said that China "would never allow this to happen."
At the same time, Stubb emphasized that Europe must be prepared for the worst-case scenario in order to prevent it.

articles.title: Sweden to Deploy Gripen Fighter Jets and Naval Ships to Guard Finnish Border With Russia
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Sweden to Deploy Gripen Fighter Jets and Naval Ships to Guard Finnish Border With Russia
The Swedish government has decided to send military units to Finland to strengthen patrolling operations along the border with Russia.
According to Swedish public broadcaster SVT on August 28, the action comes after a direct request from Finnish authorities for military assistance to respond to ongoing air space threats tied to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Over the past year, Finland has recorded several instances of Ukrainian drones straying into its territory due to electronic warfare, alongside repeated air space violations by Russian military aircraft.
To handle these security concerns, the Swedish Armed Forces will soon deploy JAS 39 Gripen fighter jets and naval vessels to patrol regions along the Finnish-Russian border.
Additional ground support may also follow later in the year. Swedish air defense and counter-drone units could be sent to Finland during the autumn if the operational situation requires further force integration.
The entire deployment is organized alongside NATO and relies on bilateral agreements between the two nations. These legal frameworks give the Swedish government the mandate to deploy armed forces directly for the defense of Finnish territorial integrity.
This operation sits within a larger expansion of regional security ties in Northern Europe. Sweden is set to assume command of NATO forward land forces in Finland, where international troops will form a core element of the alliance's enhanced defense presence.
This framework includes a primary battalion task group stationed in Finland alongside a permanent multinational headquarters.
Previously, Sweden's parliamentary defense commission warned in a report covered by Bloomberg on June 12 that Russia could seek to test NATO's cohesion and commitment to mutual defense through a military attack in the "relatively near term."

Senator Elizabeth Warren calls Trump ‘the most corrupt president ever in American history’
TEHRAN — US Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren has delivered a scathing critique of President Donald Trump, labeling him "the most corrupt president ever in American history" and accusing major energy corporations aligned with his administration of reaping vast financial gains from the military conflict against Iran.
Speaking at an election campaign rally for a junior senator from Massachusetts, Warren emphasized that oil executives who poured millions into political campaigns are now extracting massive corporate windfall earnings as energy costs skyrocket for ordinary working families. She pointed out that the single fastest path to relieving energy burdens on everyday citizens is to halt military operations in the region immediately, declaring that ending the campaign in Iran would instantly lower fuel prices at home. “So the question becomes: What do we do about that? When Donald Trump starts a war with Iran and his oil buddies, who gave him a million dollars for his campaign—when they start making profits like crazy, then our job is to call it out and fight back. That’s what we do,” Warren told the roaring crowd during her address. “You want to lower the price of gasoline? End the war in Iran. Just end it,” she added, directly challenging the White House's foreign policy rationale.
The senator's blunt assessment comes alongside recent official financial disclosure filings showing that Trump continues to hold and actively trade stock portfolios in major natural gas and petroleum giants. While White House spokespersons maintain that these portfolio movements operate independently of presidential oversight, political analysts and watchdog organizations highlight the undeniable conflict of interest in overseeing a massive military operation while maintaining tens of millions of dollars in personal equity tied directly to energy conglomerates that profit from wartime market volatility.
Financial data analyzed by congressional committees reveals that major US oil corporations—including ExxonMobil and Chevron—have seen their quarterly earnings multiply dramatically since the outbreak of hostilities, with corporate profits topping tens of billions of dollars and driving executive net worth to historic highs. Senate Joint Economic Committee reports indicate that Trump's personal energy portfolio alone has surged in value by over $15 million during the conflict, growing by an average of nearly 40 percent since the beginning of the year. Inside the US Congress, a steadily growing coalition of anti-war lawmakers and progressive representatives has voiced fierce opposition to the administration's aggressive policy in West Asia, strongly condemning the unprovoked and illegal nature of the military actions.
Opponents in Capitol Hill argue that the executive branch deliberately bypassed constitutional war powers requirements to embark on a disastrous military campaign that severely jeopardizes international stability, harms America's standing on the global stage, and serves narrow corporate interests over the welfare of the American public. Members of Congress are demanding an immediate cessation of offensive military funding and an end to weapon transfers, asserting that hundreds of billions of taxpayer dollars currently being spent on overseas military interventions must instead be redirected toward fixing crumbling domestic infrastructure, expanding healthcare access, and alleviating the severe economic burdens faced by working families at home.
The broader international crisis stems from the joint military operations initiated by US and Israeli forces against Iran on February 28, targeting military sites and civil infrastructure, including residential area. Iranian defense forces responded under international frameworks of self-defense as recognized by Article 51 of the United Nations Charter, deploying advanced missile capabilities and maritime operational measures to neutralize hostile targets, protect territorial integrity, and assert strict defensive control over critical strategic transit corridors such as the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran has repeatedly affirmed its right to defend its territory against foreign hostility, maintaining that regional security must be governed by regional nations without imperialist interference.
Six months into the military campaign, the US armed forces face operational constraints, highlighted by the rapid depletion of critical precision-guided munition stockpiles, Patriot interceptors, and complex air defense systems. US defense industrial supply chains continue to struggle under severe structural bottlenecks and material shortages, rendering the rapid replenishment of key military hardware functionally impossible in the short term. At the same time, the broader American domestic economy suffers from persistent inflation, soaring pump prices, rising shipping fees, and expanding public debt, leaving working-class citizens to bear the financial costs of an overextended foreign policy. Public dissatisfaction across major cities continues to surge as critics point out the glaring contrast between unlimited funding for foreign military actions and the neglected needs of the domestic population.

articles.title: The Third World War may be fought with weapons built in garages
articles.body:
The Third World War may be fought with weapons built in garages
“And out of the smoke locusts came down on the earth and were given power like that of scorpions of the earth…” – Revelation 9:3-5.
NATO has reportedly drawn up a plan for war with Russia in the event of a Russian attack on the Baltic states. At first glance, the document might seem unremarkable given the most senior officer involved in preparing it holds the rank of major, because every year, Russian and American military academies produce hundreds of officers capable of writing plans of this sort.
But two things make it worth paying attention to. The first is that modern military science is undergoing a profound crisis and the old methods of warfare are becoming increasingly difficult to use. Tank breakthroughs, deep encirclements and prolonged artillery barrages are all far more dangerous than they were even a decade ago because the battlefield is saturated with unmanned aerial vehicles.
The second is more surprising as military plans for a potential war aren’t usually made public, therefore NATO appears to be sending a message that we understand how warfare has changed, and we’re preparing for it.
The outlines of a possible non-nuclear Third World War can already be seen in such planning, but that assumes, of course, that nuclear powers could become involved in a global confrontation without crossing the nuclear threshold, instead fighting through local allies and proxies. What stands out in the NATO concept is the central role given to robotic and autonomous systems.
Fully autonomous warfare still belongs partly to the future, but even remotely controlled systems have already changed tactics more dramatically than almost any military innovation of the modern era. The closest historical comparison may be the arrival of rifled weapons, when massed column attacks became suicidal.
Only a few years ago, tanks were still regarded as the decisive instrument of land warfare, yet today a tank may struggle even to reach its firing position because the approaches are covered by drones, including so-called ‘waiters’ that land, remain concealed, and take off only when ordered to attack.
Technology has changed the battlefield with extraordinary speed and now NATO has published a defense concept for the three small Baltic states that appears to acknowledge this new reality. The importance of the document lies less in the rank of the officers who drafted it than in the fact that the alliance is publicly demonstrating its readiness for a different kind of war.I suspect that was the main reason for publishing it and the message is directed at an adversary that already has four years of intensive combat experience. The contours of a future non-nuclear world war are therefore becoming clearer. I’m not a military specialist, so I will speak only in broad terms. Human soldiers may increasingly be concentrated in elite formations and special forces, while much of the conventional battlefield is handed over to machines.
Back in the late 1980s, a special forces officer once told me that such units were becoming less useful when employed in support of large conventional armies and he predicted a gradual decline in the importance of elite formations, but history may now be turning in the opposite direction.
Perhaps the armies of the future will consist largely of small groups of highly trained soldiers operating in support of vast numbers of robotic systems. Drones have already transformed warfare and artificial intelligence and autonomous platforms may transform it far more radically.If that happens, enormous armies could become obsolete and inflicting strategic damage on an enemy may no longer require columns of armored vehicles or millions of soldiers. Nor would it necessarily require the gigantic defense-industrial complexes familiar from the 20th century as much of the equipment could be cheap and rapidly replaceable.
Even today, effective drones can be assembled in a garage, but of course, future combat systems will require increasingly sophisticated electronics, although it’s not yet clear how different many of those components will be from technologies already used in smartphones and consumer electronics.
This would also change the nature of military targets, for why attack an enemy’s tanks if you can disable the electricity that allows its entire military system to function?
Power stations will inevitably become heavily protected, but transmission networks are much more difficult to defend and it’s impossible to guard every kilometer of high-voltage cable. This could lead to a new emphasis on dispersed electricity generation and the Soviet Union already experimented with unconventional solutions in remote northern regions, including the use of nuclear technology originally developed for submarines. The economics of war would change as well given that drones are operated by small teams – or eventually by autonomous systems – and are cheap compared to the industrial machinery of traditional warfare.
 They also reduce the enormous logistical burden associated with artillery, where a shell must be manufactured, transported by rail, moved again by truck and finally delivered to a gun. Even then, dozens or hundreds may need to be fired to destroy a single target. The scale of traditional warfare is difficult to comprehend. During one offensive in the First World War, the Entente fired roughly 25 million artillery shells, while the Central Powers mobilized about the same number of men over the entire conflict.
Modern precision weapons are far more effective, but they are also increasingly expensive, and massed artillery itself is becoming vulnerable to drones and counter-battery systems. That’s why the Third World War, if it comes, may look nothing like the previous two.It may not begin with millions of soldiers crossing borders or vast tank armies moving across Europe. Instead, it could consist of many simultaneous regional conflicts fought by smaller allies of nuclear powers, while the great powers themselves remain protected beneath their nuclear umbrellas.
A future world war may therefore not be one enormous battlefield but dozens of smaller ones, connected by drones, satellites, artificial intelligence, and the political interests of states that can’t afford to fight one another directly.
This article was first published by Gazeta.ru, translated and edited by RT team

articles.title: Minab school tragedy will never be forgotten or forgiven, Iran FM says
articles.body:
Minab school tragedy will never be forgotten or forgiven, Iran FM says
TEHRAN- Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the tragedy at a school in Minab, southern Iran, will never be forgotten or forgiven, describing the students killed in the incident as a symbol of heroism for the Iranian people.
Araghchi made the remarks on Friday at the opening ceremony of the group exhibition “Minab School,” held at the Art Bureau of the Islamic Ideology Dissemination Organization in Tehran.
The exhibition has been organized by the Nam Cultural and Artistic Institute and features works by a number of prominent contemporary Iranian painters.
“The students of this school have become an epic for the Iranian people. We will never forget or forgive this incident, nor will we erase it from our memory. We will continue to pursue it,” Araghchi said.
He emphasized the power of art to preserve historical events and convey messages, saying a single painting can sometimes communicate with an audience and leave an impact equivalent to several speeches and books.
“These works are documents of the legitimacy and victimhood of the Iranian people and the children who were deliberately and unjustly targeted in this war,” the foreign minister said. “Although we lost them, they have become heroic symbols for the Iranian people.”
Araghchi expressed hope that the exhibition could be taken to other countries, allowing international audiences to see the works and learn about what happened to the Iranian children.
“I hope we can take this exhibition abroad, country by country, and show it to people,” he said, adding that those who claim to defend human rights should see the artworks depicting the consequences of the conflict.
The foreign minister also highlighted the role of art in diplomacy, saying paintings, films, poetry and music can convey messages in ways that written statements and speeches often cannot.
He noted that Iranian artists produced numerous works during the recent conflicts, including music, video productions and visual artworks, stressing that such efforts should continue so that future generations and international audiences understand the sacrifices made by the Iranian people during the 12-day and 40-day wars.
Araghchi said the Foreign Ministry's public diplomacy department is responsible, among other things, for cultural and artistic diplomacy. He added that the ministry is ready to support Iranian artists and facilitate the presentation of exhibitions such as “Minab School” abroad.
He also said the Foreign Ministry's legal department has been documenting what he described as crimes committed by the United States and Israel during recent wars against Iran. According to Araghchi, four or five volumes of documentation have so far been compiled, while the ministry is continuing to document the impact of economic sanctions.
The minister criticized what he described as the politicization of human rights by Western countries, saying that while Western governments issue numerous statements concerning individual cases in Iran, they have failed to take comparable action over the deaths of Palestinians in Gaza.
“Our policy is completely clear: We genuinely believe in human rights in Iran and have always defended the rights of the Iranian people,” Araghchi said, stressing that Tehran would not allow human rights to be used as a tool for political exploitation.
The exhibition features works by artists including Behzad Shishegaran, Sirous Moqaddam, Gholam-Ali Taheri, Morteza Asadi, Kazem Chalipa, Ali Nedai, Hassan Yaqouti, Abdolhamid Ghadirian, Mostafa Goudarzi, Nasser Seifi, Jamshid Haqiqatshenas, Seyyed Masoud Shojai Tabatabai, Kamyar Sadeqi, Seyyed Ali Mirfattah, Mahyar Charmchi, Mostafa Qorbani, Hossein Einibakhsh and Mohammad-Ali Naderi.
Araghchi, Head of the Art Bureau Mohammad-Mehdi Dadman and a number of prominent visual artists attended the opening and visited the exhibition.
“Minab School” will run through September 22 at the Art Bureau, from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. daily.
On February 28, the Shajareh Tayyebeh girls' elementary school in Minab, Hormozgan province, became the site of a devastating massacre as the United States and Israel initiated their strikes against Iran.
While dozens of girls and boys aged between 7 and 12 were beginning their lessons, the school was targeted by a missile strike that caused the building to collapse, trapping children and teachers beneath the rubble. Iranian authorities confirmed a final death toll of 168 people, with at least 95 others wounded, marking one of the most harrowing incidents of the conflict's opening day.
Despite attempts by US and Israeli authorities to distance themselves from the carnage as images of the tragedy spread across social media, detailed forensic and digital investigations have painted a starkly different picture.
An analysis by Al Jazeera’s digital investigations unit, utilizing over a decade of satellite imagery and recent video clips, revealed that the school was a clearly distinct civilian facility, separated from any adjacent military sites for at least ten years. Furthermore, witness accounts and satellite-based analyses confirmed that the school was triple tapped by three separate, deliberate strikes, leaving no doubt about the nature of the attack.
The international community has faced mounting evidence regarding the responsibility for this atrocity, with investigations from major global outlets including The New York Times, BBC Verify, CBC, and NPR all concluding that the United States was responsible for the strike.
These findings have raised fundamental questions about the intelligence used to justify the bombing, as the patterns of the strike suggest a direct targeting of a civilian educational institution. The Minab school tragedy now stands as a somber testament to the immense human cost of the aggression and a focal point for those demanding international accountability.
SAB/

articles.title: Ukrainian nuclear power plant without external power for over a week
articles.body:
Ukrainian nuclear power plant without external power for over a week
This is the 27th time since Russia invaded Ukraine that the Zaporizhzhia plant has had to rely on emergency diesel supplies.
The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power station in southeastern Ukraine has been without off-site power for more than a week, the world’s nuclear energy watchdog has warned.
The plant, which Russia has occupied since 2022, is currently relying on emergency diesel generators, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said on Saturday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Zaporizhzhia’s mayor says Russian advance reaches city’s outskirts
- list 2 of 3Russia reports Ukrainian drone strike near Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant
- list 3 of 3Russia warns it could target UK in response to Kyiv firing British missiles
The plant needs power to keep its six non-operating reactors cool and has only a 10-day diesel supply on site, the IAEA said in a statement.
“The availability of diesel fuel is of paramount importance whenever a nuclear power plant loses off-site power,” IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said.
The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant has not had a delivery from an off-site storage facility in about six months but was supplied with diesel on Thursday and Friday from another off-site location, the IAEA said.
The Vienna-based agency is now trying to negotiate a local ceasefire to allow repairs to electrical lines.
Zaporizhzhia is Europe’s largest nuclear power plant. It has not generated electricity since September 2022, over six months after Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February that year, but the plant’s reactors must be kept cool to prevent a meltdown of the fuel inside.
“This is the 27th blackout at the plant since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion,” Ukraine’s deputy head of military law enforcement, Gyunduz Mamedov, wrote on X on Saturday.
The IAEA has had a permanent presence at the site since September 2022, after Russia took control of the Ukrainian facility in March that year.
Both sides in the conflict regularly accuse the other of attacking the site, which sits on the banks of the Dnipro River and demarcates the front line in the sector.
On Friday, the IAEA said there had been three incidents that week with drones at the plant, injuring two employees. It did not say who launched the drones.
Earlier this month, a drone strike close to the plant killed one nuclear specialist and wounded 17, with Moscow asserting that Kyiv was behind the attack.
Ukrainian officials have repeatedly warned that Russian actions in and around the plant constitute nuclear blackmail against Ukraine and Europe more widely.
In 2024, footage emerged of a fire in one of the power plant’s cooling towers, prompting Ukraine to accuse Russia of nuclear blackmail.
