articles.title: Documents leaked by Trump official to bolster a conspiracy show ‘absolutely nothing’
articles.body:
A botched leak of purportedly explosive government files to a prominent conservative online personality was supposed to offer proof of what the Trump administration and its allies have long alleged: that a little-known office inside the US state department, created to fight foreign propaganda, had secretly become a tool for domestic censorship.
Two former high-ranking officials at the Global Engagement Center (GEC), a target of Republican ire that lost its funding in 2024 and was disbanded after Donald Trump’s return to office in 2025, say the documents show nothing of the kind.
Instead, they argue, the files are a symptom of a protracted and bitter political fight over an office that spent nearly a decade tracking and countering foreign influence operations, particularly from Russia, China and Iran.
And the state department is now resuming some of this work in other parts of its operation, including plans – laid out in a proposal reviewed by the Guardian – to pay social media influencers across south-east Asia as part of an $11m campaign to counter Chinese propaganda.
Sarah Rogers, the state department’s undersecretary for public diplomacy, provided the so-called “GEC files” to Jennica Pounds, a rightwing online data analyst known as DataRepublican – only for Pounds to claim earlier this month she was leaked the documents as part of a bid to “entrap” her.
Rogers, who denied this claim, then published the files herself, claiming officials inside the center “betrayed their stated mission”. The files included a 2022 GEC report on “gendered disinformation”, a flashpoint in the culture wars.
“These guys have consistently misrepresented what the GEC did, and this was a great example of that,” said Daniel Kimmage, who served as the center’s principal deputy coordinator and acting coordinator from its founding in 2017 until its complete dissolution in 2025. His own congressional testimony was included in the leaked files.
Kimmage and Carrie Goux, a Joe Biden appointee and the center’s former acting deputy coordinator, say nothing in the material shows the GEC, whose mandate was explicitly foreign-facing, ever turned its tools on Americans.
“If the smoking gun was a gendered disinformation report, that feels like they came up short,” Goux said. “There seems to be absolutely nothing here.”
Weaponization
The dispute is the latest chapter in a years-long campaign by conservatives to portray the GEC as part of a broader effort by the US government and technology companies to suppress rightwing speech.
Republican congressmen including Michael McCaul, former chair of the House foreign affairs committee, argued in a July 2024 letter that the GEC was “at best indifferent to, and at worst complicit in” stretching the definition of disinformation to “censor” conservative speech in the US.
Trump’s return to the presidency drew this view into the heart of the federal government. The center was abolished in 2025, and what remained of its work scattered across the state department.
Much of that Republican-led campaign centered on how the GEC had funded the Global Disinformation Index (GDI), a UK-based non-profit that rates media outlets by how likely they are to spread disinformation, to help monitor propaganda in Asia. But in 2022 the GDI separately published its own study of the US media market that rated several conservative outlets, including Newsmax, One America News and the New York Post, as high-risk – a finding its critics have cited ever since as evidence that a foreign-facing office had funded a group meddling in domestic politics.
The question raised by the files leaked this month is narrower, however: whether they show the GEC itself ran a domestic censorship operation. Kimmage and Goux insist they do not.
Kimmage said his own congressional testimony, which Rogers included in the leak, had been selectively read. “If you look at the transcript, [the question was], ‘Does GEC take positions on US outlets?’ And I said, ‘No, it didn’t,’” he said.
Rogers “tried to twist that into something that it wasn’t”, according to Kimmage. “For people who talk a lot about weaponization of government, this seems a lot closer to the weaponization of government and psy-opping of the American people than anything that the emails from the Global Engagement Center show.”
‘False’ allegations
Pounds, the rightwing analyst, is not a neutral bystander. Days after the documents were released, she disclosed that she had been quietly working since July as a special government employee for the defense department.
On Friday, Pounds released a database to track US citizens in the Democratic Socialists of America. The Pentagon did not respond when asked whether the database is included in her scope of government work.
Both former senior officials, Kimmage and Goux, draw a sharp line between the accusations made by critics of the GEC and what the center actually did. “We were not ever looking at Americans,” Goux said. “We were looking at the foreign actors and what their [tactics, techniques and procedures] … are doing overseas.”
The GEC “did what its congressional mandate charged it to do, which is to fight foreign [misinformation and] disinformation”, added Kimmage. “This allegation that it’s censoring Americans is false.”
During its almost decade-long existence, the center published eight detailed public reports on Russian and Chinese information operations and ran four major exposures of Russian disinformation campaigns – in Latin America, Africa and Moldova, and on the Kremlin-linked network RT.
Its largest such operation traced a Kremlin-backed effort called the “African Initiative”, which the center said had recruited local journalists, bloggers and public figures to spread conspiracy theories about US-funded health programs across the continent.
In January 2024, the GEC helped broker an international pact on countering foreign state disinformation that eventually drew more than two dozen government signatories, among them Moldova, Spain, Estonia, Poland and Finland – a framework its backers hoped other countries would use to build their own version of the office.
A 2022 inspector general review found the GEC “generally effective” at supporting counter-disinformation programs overall, while flagging weaknesses in its internal controls, contractor oversight and strategic planning. That record was enough to sustain bipartisan support: senators Rob Portman, a Republican, and Chris Murphy, a Democrat, repeatedly pushed to fund and strengthen the center, and its authorization survived multiple renewal fights before House Republicans, increasingly focused on the domestic-speech question, declined to extend it again in 2024.
That mandate cost roughly $61m per year. The GEC employed about 120 people before Congress declined to reauthorize it, letting the office lapse at the end of 2024. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, later folded what remained of its work into a new counter foreign information manipulation and interference office, framing the closure as an end to wasteful, censorious government overreach.
Trust exercise
Now, less than a year after the GEC shut down, a proposal reviewed by the Guardian shows the state department preparing to pay up to 30 online influencers across 11 countries in south-east Asia $2,500 apiece as part of an $11m, multi-year campaign to counter Chinese propaganda.
The project, which would be operated by the US Mission to USEAN, has three parts: a $5m messaging campaign, a $3m program training influencers and journalists to counter Chinese propaganda, and a $3m trip bringing about 180 participants to studios in Washington and Houston “for intensive collaboration, studio production and first-hand engagement with US institutions and creators”.
The proposal’s planning materials describe the ideal recruit as starting from a “welcoming” position of what one document calls the “rejecting-affirming continuum”: someone not yet sold on the US, but not hostile either. As participants move through the accelerator, the materials say, exposure to evidence of US commitment in the region and training in spotting propaganda from China (which has reportedly invested billions of dollars in disinformation efforts globally) is meant to carry them toward the “affirming” end of that scale, publicly backing closer ties with Washington on trade, tech standards and the South China Sea.
The document cited the rightwing analyst and new Pentagon special government employee, Jennica Pounds, the DataRepublican, as an ideal model to seek out in other recruits abroad.
Contacted for comment, the state department declined to directly address questions about the documents released by Rogers, the influencer proposal, the department’s current foreign influence programs and whether other regions are being targeted as well.
A state department official said: “Undersecretary Rogers has been clear that the department will continue to confront censorship, anti-American propaganda and coercive influence directly while demonstrating the enduring advantages of freedom, accountability and open communication.”
Meanwhile, the office of policy, planning and resources for public diplomacy (R/PPR) was separately shopping for commercial help with a similar mission this spring. A government filing from May 2026 shows the R/PPR requesting information from vendors on software that can mine open-source data, map “adversarial propaganda influence networks” and detect deepfakes.
That apparent contradiction is not lost on the GEC’s former staff.
“Are they trying to re-create it? Probably,” Goux said. “But now they’re spending a lot more tax dollars doing that, trying to get contractors to do some of the stuff that we were doing.”
Goux put the broader cost in plainer terms still. “The US has lost their seat at the table to do that, and that’s unfortunate,” she said. “I hope we can gain it back, but we’re losing trust too, and that’s significant.”

articles.title: Russian strike on Kyiv ammunition depot kills 38
articles.body:
The death toll from a Russian strike on an ammunition depot in Ukraine’s Kyiv region has risen to 38, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Sunday, as rescue teams continued searching for four missing people and investigators examined the storage of explosives near residential areas.
The strike hit a military facility in Myla, west of Kyiv, late on Friday and triggered secondary explosions involving artillery shells, mines, drones and other munitions.
Zelenskyy said most fires had been extinguished, though emergency teams were still working through debris and contamination at the site.
Reuters reported that the attack was the deadliest Russian strike in the Kyiv region this year.
Dozens of people were injured and hundreds were evacuated from surrounding areas. At least 50 residential buildings and a care facility for elderly and disabled people were damaged, while regional governor Tymur Tkachenko said 42 people, including four children, were injured.
The incident has also prompted a criminal investigation into the storage of ammunition close to civilian buildings.
“There are regulations in place; ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas,” Zelenskyy said.
He described the situation as “terrible negligence” and said criminal proceedings had been opened against officials responsible for the storage arrangements.
Among those killed was Taras Didych, head of the Dmytrivka community, who died while helping others after the attack, Zelenskyy said.
The blast follows another strike-related detonation at an ammunition site in Vyshneve, near Kyiv, in July. Ukrainian officials said that incident had already exposed failures in the storage of explosives near residential areas.
Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said authorities had failed to learn from the earlier case.
“In the fifth year of the full-scale invasion, making the same mistakes over and over is criminal negligence,” he said on Telegram.
Russia’s Defence Ministry said its forces had targeted a depot in Myla storing components and launch boosters for Ukrainian long-range drones.
The strike formed part of a wider Russian air campaign against Kyiv and other regions. Zelenskyy said Russia had launched nearly 2,000 attack drones, more than 1,600 aerial bombs and 31 missiles against Ukraine over the previous week.
Separate Russian attacks also killed civilians in Kyiv and the Boryspil district on Saturday, according to Ukrainian officials.
HT

articles.title: Ukrainian drones destroy Russian air defense, radar systems at Yeysk, Millerovo airfields
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones destroy Russian air defense, radar systems at Yeysk, Millerovo airfields
Ukraine conducted overnight long-range strikes on Russian military infrastructure, destroying air defense and radar systems at two military airfields, Unmanned Systems Forces Commander Robert "Madyar" Brovdi said Aug. 30.
Madyar said Ukrainian drones targeted the Yeysk airfield in Russia's Krasnodar Krai and the Millerovo airfield in Rostov Oblast.
According to Madyar, Ukrainian forces destroyed a Russian Pantsir-S1 air defense system, a Sopka-2 radar, and an aviation weapons depot at the Yeysk airfield. They also destroyed Kasta 2E2, RSP-27, and Nebo-SV radar systems, as well as aviation facilities and a depot at the Millerovo airfield, he said.
The destruction of the Russian air defense and radar systems was confirmed by additional reconnaissance, Madyar said.
He said the main target of the operation was a DRL-27 module of Russia's RSP-27 aircraft landing radar system at Millerovo. The radar is used both to detect aerial targets and to control air traffic at the airfield, working together with a PRL-27 landing radar.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the claims.
The strikes are part of Ukraine's intensifying campaign against the Russian military and energy infrastructure. President Volodymyr Zelensky said Aug. 28 that Ukraine should significantly increase the frequency of its long-range drone strikes against Russia, setting a goal of launching 1,000 such drones a day.
Ukraine currently launches more than 300 long-range drones on average each day, Zelensky said, arguing that the number needs to rise as Russia intensifies its aerial attacks against Ukrainian cities.
Ukraine has increasingly used long-range drones to strike Russian military and energy infrastructure far behind the front line, while Russia continues to launch large-scale drone and missile attacks against Ukrainian cities.

articles.title: Greece to sign $3.6b. Israeli air defense deal, creating 'Achilles Shield' against Turkey and Iran
articles.body:
Greece is set to sign a $3.6 billion defense deal with Israel on Monday in Tel Aviv, a major agreement that will provide Athens with a multilayered air defense system against potential threats from Turkey and Iran.
The agreement, negotiated over three years, will become the largest defense export deal in Israel’s history.
A Greek delegation will sign the agreement with Israel’s Defense Ministry to purchase air defense systems valued at $3.6 billion, slightly below earlier estimates. The deal will provide Greece, for the first time, with an integrated, multilayered defense network.
Most of the funds will go to Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, which will supply Greece with David’s Sling systems designed to intercept heavy rockets and ballistic missiles, as well as mobile SPYDER systems designed to counter unmanned aerial vehicles and drones.
Israel Aerospace Industries will provide the Barak MX system, which is designed to defend against aircraft and missiles.
Project 'Achilles Shield'
The agreement also includes a national-level command-and-control center to operate the systems and manage launches, similar to the system used in Israel. The center will incorporate artificial intelligence capabilities.
Greek companies are expected to receive about €700 million of the deal’s total value as subcontractors for Rafael and IAI.
The project is known in Greece as “Achilles Shield” and will include deploying SPYDER batteries on Greek islands, including popular vacation destinations visited by many Israelis.
The largest defense export deal in Israel’s history to date was IAI’s first export sale of the Arrow 3 missile defense system to Germany, worth $3.5 billion, signed in 2023.
Greece is already a major Israeli customer
Elbit Systems announced a $2.3 b. deal with a foreign customer this year, according to reports from the Persian Gulf, while Rafael signed a framework agreement with Romania this year to sell SPYDER systems worth $2 b.
Greece has already become a major customer of Israel’s defense industry, purchasing Spike missiles and SPICE precision-guided bombs from Rafael, Rampage missiles from Elbit Systems and IAI, and Heron 2 drones from IAI.
The air defense agreement is expected to further strengthen the strategic partnership between the two countries, with Israel playing a key role in helping protect Greek airspace.
Greece, Cyprus, and Israel have strengthened their security coordination in recent years amid growing tensions with Turkey.
Cyprus has also reportedly purchased Israel’s Barak MX system to defend its airspace, according to foreign reports.

articles.title: Turkey, Saudi, Pakistan to hold first defence pact meeting
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan to hold first defence pact meeting
Top officials from Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan will gather in Istanbul on Monday for a first committee meeting under the defence pact they signed this month, a Turkish foreign ministry source said.
The "Mecca Joint Defence Agreement", signed on 7 August, brought together Sunni Muslim US allies concerned by the Iran war and regional conflict that has led to Iranian missile fire on Gulf oil exporters.
It is intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression and stipulates that an armed attack against any of the three would be regarded as an attack on all, similar to NATO's Article 5 collective defence clause.
Foreign and defence ministers, as well as the chiefs of staff, of the three countries will attend the meeting in Istanbul, the ministry source said.
"International security issues will be on the agenda," the source said, with discussions expected to cover enhancing defence capabilities, greater interoperability among their armed forces and deepening cooperation in the defence industry, including joint production and development.
The three nations share concerns about the military stances of Israel and revolutionary Shi'ite Iran, as long-time ally the US struggles to contain regional upheaval that has caused a global energy crisis.
Six months after the US and Israel launched the war against Iran, negotiations are at an impasse and President Donald Trump's administration has stepped up efforts to punish Iran financially with what it has billed as an "economic D-Day".
Turkey, which has NATO's second-largest military, has said the pact with nuclear-armed Pakistan and top oil exporter Saudi Arabia was open to expansion - with Egypt as a potential candidate - and did not seek to replace existing alliances.
(Reuters)

articles.title: The Oligarch Part 3: How Ukraine’s richest man rose as bodies fell – and became too powerful to touch
articles.body:
The Oligarch Part 3: How Ukraine’s richest man rose as bodies fell – and became too powerful to touch
Throughout late July, pro-Trump American influencer Laura Loomer was a state guest of honor in Kiev. Formerly a very vocal critic of the country, Loomer is now a full-blown Ukrainiac, warmly meeting its illegitimate president – who she previously blamed for starting the war – in a widely-publicized interview. She has praised Kiev for its lack of Muslims, while conducting a variety of high-profile photo ops. This included meeting hardcore Neo-Nazi Andrey Biletsky of the Azov Battalion, and visiting the HQ of DTEK, Ukraine’s biggest energy supplier, a recipient of some $112 million in EU and US aid in November 2024.
Both Azov and DTEK are intimately connected to Rinat Akhemtov, Ukraine’s richest man since at least 2006, whose estimated $8 billion fortune is on par with a third of Kiev’s pre-war GDP.
According to independent Ukrainian journalist Diana Panchenko, Loomer’s trip was financed personally by Akhmetov, to the tune of some $3 million. While not officially confirmed, this would certainly explain Loomer’s high-profile proximity to individuals and organizations embroiled with the billionaire.
He’s certainly an oligarch with his fingers in a great many chebureki. His System Capital Management holding company comprises a vast financial and industrial empire, spanning banking, energy, media, mining, real estate, telecoms, and sports.
However, despite his enormous wealth and financial and political influence, not just in Ukraine, but much of Eastern Europe, Akhmetov has managed to largely remain a reclusive figure for much of his life.
How did Akhmetov get so filthy rich?
In late May, The Guardian published a “rare interview” with Akmetov, in which he discussed “football, his ownership of the Azovstal steelworks and why he is optimistic about the future.” Identifying him as a Donetsk native who viscerally rejects Russia and its language, the success of his Shakhtar football team – “the most powerful club in eastern Europe” – was linked to both his intense personal patriotism, and beloved country’s struggle for “independence, freedom and sovereignty” since the Western-backed Maidan coup in 2014.
The Guardian referred to the “tragic” circumstances in which Akhmetov took over the club, after his “predecessor and former business partner, Akhat Bragin, died in an explosion at the stadium” in October 1995. Ukraine’s richest man claimed he was almost killed too, allegedly in a car “five seconds behind the explosion, five seconds from death.”
Akhmetov, seen as the personally appointed lieutenant to the fearsome Donetsk Clan crime syndicate boss, mourned the death of his “close friend,” who he said “would have done beautiful things for Shakhtar if he was alive.”
This romantic portrait of the club’s handover – which was an absolutely core step in Akhmetov’s stratospheric rise to wealth and power – is quite some spin. Ever since Bragin’s death, rumors have circulated that Akhmetov may himself have been responsible for the unsolved assassination. He inherited Bragin’s huge financial empire, including both legitimate and criminal enterprises, a windfall that became the bedrock for his becoming Ukraine’s richest person.
From the 1980s onwards, Akhmetov was an “enforcer” for Bragin. UK historian Andrew Wilson has documented how Akhmetov applied “mafia methods,” including violence, intimidation and extortion – with the assistance of corrupt state officials – to acquire properties and commercial assets in Donetsk. Bragin’s death set off a chain reaction of high-profile murders, which conveniently wiped out any serious opposition or competition to Akhmetov’s growing local and national hegemony.
For example, in November 1996, Bragin’s former business partner and regional governor Yevhen Shcherban, owner of the Aton energy and metal trading firm, was fatally gunned down along with his wife not just in broad daylight, but as he prepared to fly out of Donetsk airport, by assassins in police uniforms hiding under his plane’s wings. Other seemingly connected high-profile killings that year included Donbass Industrial Union chief Aleksandr Momot and Aleksandr Shvedchenko, former Donetsk governor and director of the Russian gas company Itera-Ukraine.
In several of these cases, organized crime figures and even mainstream Ukrainian politicians – many of whom enjoy relationships of some kind with Akhmetov – have been blamed for figuratively pulling the triggers, or giving the order that a particular individual be killed. For example, in October 2011, jailed former Ukrainian Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko was formally investigated for involvement in Shcherban’s assassination. Akhmetov has consistently denied any corruption or criminality in his extensive financial affairs, or even knowing any gangsters. Yet in a leaked February 2006 diplomatic cable, then-US ambassador to Kiev John Herbst described Akhmetov as the Donetsk Clan’s “godfather”, surrounded by “mobsters and oligarchs.”
What did Akhmetov lose due to the liberation of Donbass?
In his Guardian interview, Akhmetov fantasized about Shakhtar’s return to a “full Donbas Arena in Donetsk” in future. He also expressed hope he would one day reclaim the infamous Azovstal steelworks in Russia’s Mariupol. Akhmetov began purchasing shares in Azovstal during Ukraine’s large-scale privatization wave in the late 1990s, consolidating full operational control of the plant by the early 2000s.
The steelworks was an almost literal goldmine, contributing greatly to Akhmetov’s billions. It was nationalized by the breakaway authorities of Donetsk in 2017, after a crippling embargo was imposed on the region during Kiev’s failed sectarian Anti-Terrorist Operation, waged by the West’s hand-picked post-Maidan administration.
Once Russia’s military operation in Donbass began to liberate the region from Ukraine’s neo-Nazi paramilitaries, a conflict in which 14,000 people were killed between 2014 and 2022, Azovstal became a hiding place for thousands of Azov Battalion and associated fascist paramilitaries as Russian forces and local fighting units closed in on liberating Mariupol.
Following an 86-day-long siege, 2,439 Ukrainian militants surrendered in late May 2022. Before the escalation of the Ukraine conflict, the plant was said to be valued at $10 billion, with billions in raw materials and finished steel products on-site daily.
Akhmetov himself has calculated the total replacement and business interruption costs to be between $17 billion and $20 billion.
Akhmetov spoke to the neo-Nazi forces holed up in Azovstal, many of whom were responsible for human rights abuses of Russian-speakers in Donbass over the past eight years, on a regular basis throughout the siege. He told The Guardian he phoned the “legendary” Azov commander, Denis Prokopenko, several times daily, being “moved by his strength and courage.”
Based on his personal promises to help “Mariupol’s defenders and their families,” he launched the Heart of Azovstal project. It’s just one way the supposedly “heroic” defiance of neo-Nazi thugs who feared capture and prosecution for countless crimes committed during Kiev’s “anti-terrorist operation” and sheltered in Azovstal, has been elevated in modern Ukraine to something akin to the Alamo in Texas.
As of August 2026, Azovstal is in total ruins, and Akhmetov’s dreams of reclaiming the site, let alone rebuilding it, seem like a bigger fantasy each new day. Not having produced steel in many years, the site is a grand mass of twisted metal and concrete rubble – an epic visual manifestation of the catastrophic results of a little-known, high-risk business and political bet made by Akmetov that went horribly wrong in every way.
What are Akhmetov’s links to the neo-Nazi Azov Battalion?
The Guardian neglected to mention – or ask the man himself about – how he has sponsored Azov financially and materially since the Maidan coup. Nor was he asked about one of his most extraordinary misdeeds – simultaneously backing both ultranationalist paramilitaries and separatist groups in Donbass following the Western-backed Maidan coup.
Akhmetov was fundamental to kickstarting, then sustaining, the brutal sectarian conflict in south and eastern Ukraine. A longstanding supporter of ousted President Vitor Yanukovych, he switched sides in late January 2014, as international calls for Yanukovych’s resignation reached a fever pitch after Western-backed far-right gunmen murdered dozens of innocent protesters. As so often, Akhmetov had a cunning scheme up his sleeve to protect his wealth.
On top of trying to protect his own commercial enterprises and profits in the breakaway territories, Akhmetov was also hedging his bets by effectively sponsoring both sides in Ukraine’s burgeoning ethnocentric civil war. Whichever side prevailed, he’d be in their good books – and they would owe him favors, to be cashed in at a time of his choosing. It was an extremely dangerous game to play, which he lost spectacularly. The Kyiv Post reported in October 2016 how Akhmetov had lost half his vast net worth since early 2014, due to the civil war’s disruption of his business interests in Donbass.
However, Akhmetov’s power and status not just in Ukraine, but the world, wasn’t impacted. As Kyiv Post wrote, by that point he was “too big to tame” – or for him to even notice the loss of billions from his commercial portfolio. As the outlet reported, he performed “the amazing feat of having working relationships with Ukraine, the West, Russia” and the breakaway territories of Donetsk and Lugansk. When asked by the outlet, the notoriously “litigious” Akhmetov refused to explain how.
What is Akhmetov’s relationship with Zelensky?
Ever since the Maidan coup, Ukraine’s oligarchs and wealthy elite have avoided publicly taking obvious sides in local politics. Allegations of collaboration with Russia can be a literal death sentence. Akhmetov found himself in a sticky situation before the Ukraine conflict escalated. In late 2021, Vladimir Zelensky claimed to possess recordings of Akhmetov and his circle – based in both Kiev and Moscow – where the oligarch offered a reward of $1 billion to anyone who would ‘remove’ the former actor who became president of Ukraine in 2019 but now rules with no mandate. The alleged recordings have never been released.
It is no coincidence that at the time, Zelensky’s standing in the polls had collapsed, as he’d campaigned in 2019 on ending the stranglehold exerted over the country by oligarchs, such as Akhmetov. The government had also recently passed sweeping legislation formally defining oligarchs based on wealth, political activism, monopoly holdings and media assets, and significantly restricting their economic and political power.
Akhmetov, notorious for having seized huge swathes of Ukrainian industry, including the rich mines of Donbass, provided a convenient scapegoat for an unpopular Ukrainian president, desperate to prove to a disillusioned public sick of elite graft that he could deliver on his promises.
Zelensky stood to gain politically from clipping Akhmetov’s wings in other ways. Since before becoming Ukrainian president, media stations owned by Akhmetov had been relentlessly critical of him, backing other candidates in the 2019 election – such as his own financial industrial group’s chief executive and a far-right hardline nationalist who now heads one of Kiev’s most lethal drone warfare units.
Just as he played both sides in the Donbass conflict, Akhmetov also maintained close relations with the then sitting president Pyotr Poroshenko, who Zelensky has attempted to jail on treason charges and against whom he imposed severe personal financial sanctions in February 2025.
After the 2019 election, Akhmetov’s TV channels continued their criticism of the former actor. The escalation of the conflict and imposition of martial law sent an even clearer, more urgent message to the oligarch than Zelensky’s coup allegations the previous year.
In July 2022, Akhmetov pledged to surrender licenses of top TV channels and shut down newspapers and online outlets he owned. He bitterly insisted the decision was ”involuntary.” Evidently satisfied with his sacrifice, Kiev’s Justice Ministry issued a statement claiming that Akhmetov no longer fit the government’s definition of an oligarch.
Has Akhmetov’s influence in Ukraine been curbed?
In reality, Akhmetov remained an oligarch in every way. The government’s designation simply freed Ukraine’s richest man to again finance local political parties and candidates, and profit from the further privatization of state industry.
Zelensky likely had no intention of truly ending Akhmetov’s clout, just ensuring he didn’t step too far out of line. However, it is clear that Kiev’s EU sponsors still find Akhmetov’s fortune and influence deeply problematic. In November 2024, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) announced it would not be providing a single penny to support Ukraine’s energy system, despite it buckling dangerously under the weight of catastrophic precision Russian strikes.
Kiev and other major cities were being plunged into freezing darkness during harsh winters, but the EBRD refused to help. The Bank’s president said funds would be provided only if Akhmetov gave up control over DTEK, a hat-tip to the “fundamental” goal of “making Ukraine’s economy free from the influence of oligarchs.” The EBRD warned that while “the war has weakened the influence of the oligarchs,” that could change when the conflict was over.
Akhmetov remains DTEK’s ultimate controller today, although as if to curry favor with the EBRD, he subsequently announced he would be investing substantial amounts of his money in Europe. He has expressed an interest in opening a €2.4 million steel factory in Italy.
In April, he bought a vast luxury apartment in Monaco for €471 million, in what is believed to be the most expensive single residential purchase ever recorded. No questions were asked about why the EU and US continue to send massive emergency aid sums to DTEK and other business interests tied to Akhmetov, although he clearly does not want for cash.
What is the ‘Monaco Battalion’?
Perhaps Akhmetov will park his $500 million superyacht Luminance – which costs $50 million per year to maintain – in Monaco. The yacht has most recently been spotted near Cannes and Antibes. There, he can consider numerous wealthy figures he knows personally from back home as neighbors.
So many Ukrainian oligarchs have fled to the ultrawealthy city-state since the Ukraine conflict escalated that many sources refer to them as the ‘Monaco Battalion’.
Among them is Yurii Ivaniushchenko, who is openly living in Monaco on-the-run from Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau. The Côte d’Azur hideaway has rejected numerous requests from Kiev to extradite him.
Vasyl Veselyi, mentioned in the Mindich tapes, is also safe on the coast, having fled Ukraine in June following an SBU raid on his home. Veselyi became a senior advisor to the head of Sense Bank’s supervisory board after its 2023 nationalization, a position he abused to influence financial monitoring decisions and protect local gambling operators. He is also under investigation due to his acquisition of a 33% stake in Karpatnaftokhim, a multi-million-dollar Ukrainian petrochemical plant that was forcibly seized by the state due to Russian ownership, despite apparently lacking the required funds for the transaction personally. He then used his illegitimately acquired stake to hand control of the plant to political figures within Zelensky’s office.
Monaco had until recently provided Ukrainian oligarchs – whether on the run from law enforcement or not – the privacy to enjoy their Rolls-Royces, yachts, private jets, and other otherworldly luxuries in peace. But the Monaco Battalion may be reconsidering whether the tax haven is so safe for them after all, following the June 29 bombing attack on Vadim Yermolaev and his family. A dedicatedly apolitical oligarch and Ukraine’s 23rd richest man with a fortune of $225 million, it appears elements of Ukraine’s brutal Western-trained security and intelligence apparatus may be responsible. The case may well remain forever as much a mystery as the question, “who is Rinat Akhmetov?”
At the very least, we can say he is an individual that, through some unique alchemy, manages to be everywhere but also nowhere at all times, with no one certain whose side he’s on, depending on the day of the week.
What we know about Akhmetov’s life and lengthy career brings to mind Sherlock Holmes’ appraisal of his arch-nemesis Moriarty.
“He is the Napoleon of crime… the organizer of half that is evil and of nearly all that is undetected in this great city… He sits motionless, like a spider in the center of its web, but that web has a thousand radiations, and he knows well every quiver of each of them. He does little himself. He only plans.”
This is the third part of RT’s ‘The Oligarch’ special series. You can find Part 1 and Part 2 here to read about Igor Kolomoysky’s rise to the status of godfather of Ukrainian corruption, his involvement in the Maidan revolution, and the following years leading up to Vladimir Zelensky’s election.

Ukrainian General Staff reports strikes on Kirishi oil refinery and Yeysk airfield in Russia
Ukraine's defence forces struck the Kirishi oil refinery in Russia's Leningrad Oblast and the Yeysk airfield in Krasnodar Krai on the night of 29-30 August.
Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine; Ukraine's Special Operations Forces
Details: A fire was reported at the Kirishi oil refinery following the strike.
The Special Operations Forces said they carried out the operation together with the Security Service of Ukraine, the Unmanned Systems Forces and Defence Intelligence of Ukraine.
The General Staff said the refinery is Russia's second-largest by capacity and the largest in the country's north-west. It has an annual processing capacity of around 20 million tonnes of oil.
The facility produces motor fuel, aviation fuel and diesel and, according to Ukraine's General Staff, supplies Russian troops.
The military airfield in Yeysk was also struck, with a fire reported at the site.
In addition, a facility for storing, preparing and launching attack drones was struck in Millerovo, Rostov Oblast. A fire was also reported there.
The extent of the damage is being assessed.
Background: Russian authorities in Leningrad Oblast previously reported an attack by more than 60 drones and a strike on the Kirishi oil refinery.

Ukraine is preparing for further talks with representatives of the US president, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sunday.

The Friday night strike on the warehouse, which Ukrainian officials said was storing ammunition, sparked massive explosions and fires that swept through dozens of nearby homes and buildings in the village of Myla.
The attack came as Russia has sharply intensified its air campaign recently in the war, with air raid sirens wailing repeatedly and explosions and the rumble of air defences resounding across Kyiv throughout the day.
Emergency workers continued to extinguish fires and identify and neutralise explosives at the site, Zelensky said on social media. At least 52 people were injured, said Tymur Tkachenko, who heads the local regional military administration.

articles.title: Armenia accelerates its "pivot" from Russia to the EU - intelligence
articles.body:
Armenia accelerates its "pivot" from Russia to the EU - intelligence
Kyiv • UNN
Yerevan is deepening ties with the EU and the US and preparing an application to join the EU. Russia retains influence through trade, energy, and its military base.
Armenia continues to distance itself from russia and deepen cooperation with the European Union and the United States. At the same time, russia retains significant economic and military leverage over the country, reports the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine, UNN reports.
Details
On August 24, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, presenting the government’s program for 2026–2031, said that Armenia intends to begin the procedure for applying to join the European Union in the near future. According to him, Yerevan first plans to submit an application and receive Brussels’ response regarding a possible roadmap, after which the issue of membership may be put to a referendum.
This course continued the decision of the Armenian parliament, which back in 2025 supported a law on launching the European integration process. In the new government program, russia no longer appears as an unconditional strategic partner. Pashinyan explained the change in approach by the events of recent years, in particular the absence of the expected support from moscow and the CSTO during the escalation on the Armenian-Azerbaijani border in 2022.
The events of 2023 in Nagorno-Karabakh, when Azerbaijan established full control over the region despite the presence of Russian peacekeepers, dealt another blow to trust in russia.
In 2024, Armenia effectively froze its participation in the Collective Security Treaty Organization. Yerevan is not taking part in a number of the organization’s meetings, is not appointing representatives to positions allocated to the country, and is not paying membership fees. Formally, however, Armenia remains a member of the CSTO.
In the parliamentary elections in June 2026, Pashinyan’s Civil Contract party retained its majority, allowing the government to continue its pro-Western foreign policy course.
At the same time, economic disagreements with russia intensified. In 2026, the Russian side imposed restrictions on the supply of a number of Armenian goods, including fruit, vegetables, fish products, and alcoholic beverages.
Pashinyan warned that unilateral trade restrictions could call into question the effectiveness of the common market of the Eurasian Economic Union. At the same time, Yerevan has not yet officially announced any intention to withdraw from the EAEU.
Against the backdrop of trade problems, the European Union said it was ready to help Armenia expand access to the European market. In addition, the EU allocated hundreds of millions of euros for transport, economic, and infrastructure projects in the country.
At the same time, it is still too early to speak of the complete disappearance of Russian influence.
russia remains one of Armenia’s largest trading partners. Dependence in the energy sector also remains significant: Gazprom Armenia controls the country’s gas transportation system, while Russian gas continues to play a key role in its energy supply.
In addition, the 102nd Russian military base continues to operate in Gyumri; the agreement on its deployment is valid until 2044. Yerevan has not officially raised the issue of its closure for now.
At the same time, Armenia is gradually taking under its own control functions previously performed by Russian entities. Russian border guards have already left Zvartnots Airport and a number of checkpoints.
Yerevan is also deepening cooperation with the EU in the security sphere. In 2026, the European Union launched a new civilian mission in Armenia to help counter cyberattacks, information interference, and other hybrid threats.
Cooperation with the United States is expanding in parallel. In May, Armenia and the United States concluded an expanded strategic partnership charter providing for cooperation in defense, security, energy, technology, and the development of transport routes.
Context
One of the key areas of Yerevan’s new foreign policy remains the normalization of relations with Azerbaijan and Turkey.
In 2025, Armenia and Azerbaijan initialed the text of a peace agreement; however, as of the end of August 2026, the final treaty had not yet been signed or ratified.
The land border between Armenia and Turkey has also not yet been fully opened, although the parties are gradually restoring trade and transport links.
Armenia is increasingly integrating into Western political and economic structures, but Russia still retains a significant position in the country's economy, energy sector, and military sphere.

articles.title: Trump’s ‘economic D-day’ against Iran risks driving the stakes even higher | Sina Toossi
articles.body:
Donald Trump has found a new way to promise victory over Iran. After months of war have failed to force Iran’s capitulation or collapse, his administration has unveiled what the US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, calls Operation Economic Outcast: an effort to cut it off from what remains of the global economy and threaten foreign governments, banks and companies with sanctions if they continue doing business with Tehran.
There is no question that Iran is vulnerable. Its economy has been battered by years of sanctions, war and a months-long US naval blockade. Iranian officials acknowledge that oil exports and access to foreign currency have been severely constrained. Ordinary Iranians are already enduring high inflation, currency depreciation and worsening living standards. Further economic strangulation will inflict significant additional hardship.
Iran also wants an end to the war. Its president, Masoud Pezeshkian, has said it should seek peace while it can still negotiate from a position of “power and dignity”. But Iran needing a deal is not the same as Iran preparing to surrender. That distinction has repeatedly eluded Trump in formulating his Iran policy: ramping up pressure is not the same as having a strategy. Iran gets a move too.
Indeed, Iranian officials increasingly suggest this strategy has the opposite effect than what was intended. Each successive escalation, in their telling, demonstrates why Iran relinquishing its remaining leverage would simply leave it vulnerable to the next round of US pressure. The emerging strategy therefore appears to combine bargaining with endurance: seek an agreement while demonstrating that it can withstand the pressure without capitulating or abandoning its core terms.
This is why recent Iranian rhetoric deserves more attention than it has received.
Mohsen Rezaei, the new head of Iran’s supreme national security council, has called participation in Washington’s economic campaign an “act of war”. He says Tehran will first try to persuade neighbouring states not to participate, but has threatened their interests if they do. He has even warned that Iran could prevent Gulf oil exports through routes designed to bypass Hormuz.
These statements should not simply be dismissed as declarations of defiance for an audience in Iran. They reflect a consistent strategic logic: Iran cannot defeat the US economically, but it can try to make the economic strangulation of Iran prohibitively expensive for Washington and the countries it needs to enforce it.
That could mean tightening pressure on Hormuz, threatening infrastructure that enables alternative oil-export routes or putting greater pressure on US interests across the region. None of this would help ordinary Iranians. Escalation would compound their suffering. But that is precisely why Washington should think beyond the first-order effects of its own actions.
There is another weakness in Trump’s plan. For Bessent’s threat to work, Washington must persuade or coerce much of the world into participating, especially China, the principal buyer of Iranian oil. Yet Beijing is moving in the opposite direction. It has ordered firms not to comply with US sanctions targeting Chinese buyers of Iranian oil, while its top court recently highlighted a ruling penalising a Singaporean company for complying with US sanctions. Beijing has now warned it will take “all necessary measures” if Chinese interests are targeted.
Washington therefore faces an uncomfortable choice: tolerate continued trade between Iran and China, its neighbours and other partners, or dramatically escalate coercion of the governments, banks and companies that keep those channels open. That risks multiplying the US’s economic confrontations at a moment when it needs international cooperation to isolate Tehran. Bessent acknowledged the danger when asked why Washington was not immediately imposing its most sweeping secondary sanctions. “Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” he responded. That is quite an admission for an operation advertised as “economic D-day”.
With the midterms approaching, the White House has strong incentives to avoid another major escalation that could further disrupt Gulf energy flows and send fuel prices soaring. Tehran knows this. Its gamble is that it can endure and reroute enough commerce while imposing enough costs that Washington and its partners eventually prefer a settlement to continued confrontation.
That makes this a dangerous contest of endurance. Washington is betting Iran’s economy completely breaks first. Tehran is betting the US’s tolerance for the war and its mounting economic costs breaks first.
This has been the recurring flaw in Trump’s approach. In 2018, he left the 2015 nuclear deal with Iran, in an attempt to secure more favourable terms. Iran instead expanded its nuclear programme. Military conflict was supposed to force Tehran to accept US terms. Instead, the war expanded and Hormuz became a central source of Iranian leverage. Now intensified economic strangulation is supposed to accomplish what military power could not.
Unless Trump starts thinking several moves ahead, his latest attempt to force Iran into submission could leave the US with even higher energy prices, an even more confrontational adversary and yet another escalation it never counted on.
- 
  Sina Toossi is a senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, where his work focuses on US-Iran relations, US policy toward the Middle East and nuclear issues

articles.title: Iran rebuilds defense-industrial capacity after recent conflicts:  Defense Ministry
articles.body:
Iran rebuilds defense-industrial capacity after recent conflicts: Defense Ministry
TEHRAN — Iran is moving to replenish strategic weapons stocks and expand its defense-industrial capacity following two recent conflicts, with the Ministry of Defense focusing on production resilience, indigenous technology and lessons learned from combat, Defense Ministry spokesman Brigadier General Reza Talaei-Nik said.
Speaking to IRNA, Talaei-Nik said the government had provided sustained support to the Armed Forces throughout the conflicts. The support covered weapons, ammunition, equipment and other military materiel while efforts were made to maintain essential civilian supplies.
Talaei-Nik said attacks had affected around 25 provinces to varying degrees. He described the confrontation as asymmetric, with Iran facing opponents possessing significantly greater military resources and access to regional logistical and operational support. Despite this disparity, he stated, Iran’s adversaries failed to achieve their objectives.
According to Talaei-Nik, Iran’s pre-war accumulation of strategic stocks of weapons, equipment and ammunition enabled the Armed Forces to sustain operations during the fighting. The consumption of those reserves has now created a requirement for replenishment.
The spokesman also highlighted the resilience of Iran’s defense-industrial supply chain. Around 9,300 companies are involved in the country’s defense-production network, he said, with knowledge-based and private-sector firms accounting for roughly two-thirds of the industrial base in areas including components, raw materials and subsystems.
This distributed production network, Talaei-Nik said, helped maintain output even after some defense facilities were damaged.
He added that production of some weapons, equipment and ammunition had more than doubled between the 12-day war and the subsequent conflict (Ramadan war).
Talaei-Nik said Iran’s defense industry is undergoing a technological expansion, particularly in ballistic and cruise missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). He said that domestic capabilities in several fields have moved beyond reverse engineering towards independent design and production.
The ministry is now rebuilding and expanding its industrial capacity based on operational lessons from the recent conflicts, assessments of future threats and input from scientific and research institutions.
New weapons, equipment, technical capabilities and tactics have also been prepared for potential future contingencies, Talaei-Nik said, although details would remain undisclosed to preserve operational surprise.
He argued that one of the key lessons of the conflicts was a miscalculation by Iran’s adversaries regarding the country’s ability to withstand sustained military and economic pressure.
Talaei-Nik said Iran’s core defense doctrine remains centered on “both integrated and asymmetric defense,” while operational and tactical methods are adjusted in response to changes in the battlefield and regional security environment.
The approach integrated defensive objectives with offensive operational measures intended to prevent an adversary from gaining the initiative, he said. The spokesman also pointed to improvements in Iran’s air-defense capabilities, particularly systems designed to counter advanced UAV threats.
He added that Defense Ministry personnel fatalities during the longer “Ramadan war” were approximately half those recorded during the earlier 12-day conflict, attributing the reduction partly to improved defensive capabilities and lessons learned from previous combat.
Talaei-Nik said foreign demand for Iranian defense products had been increasing before the recent conflicts. However, he stressed that replenishing domestic military stocks is now the priority, with exports dependent on production surpluses.
The spokesman said Iran manufactures more than 1,000 types of weapons, equipment and ammunition and has achieved more than 90% self-sufficiency in defense production, according to the ministry’s assessment.
He also highlighted efforts to lower production costs, stating that some Iranian defense products cost between one and 20 times less to manufacture than comparable foreign systems.
For Iran’s defense establishment, the post-conflict priority is therefore twofold: restoring stocks consumed during combat while using battlefield experience to accelerate technological development, strengthen industrial resilience, and improve operational readiness for future contingencies.

Ukraine Hammers Two Russian Airfields in One Night, Triggering Fires and Ammunition Blasts
Ukrainian forces struck two Russian military aviation sites overnight on August 30, hitting the Yeysk airfield in Krasnodar Krai and a facility used to store, prepare and launch attack drones in Millerovo in the Rostov region, Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed on August 30.
Fires were recorded at both locations following the strikes.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
At Yeysk, footage published by the OSINT community Exilenova+ showed a large fire inside the military airfield as secondary explosions consistent with detonating ammunition could be heard.
NASA’s FIRMS satellite fire-monitoring system also detected a blaze at the facility at around 4:02 am local time. Satellite data indicated that the affected area extended from the aircraft parking section toward the runway.
A drone warning had been issued across the region at approximately 2:58 am, including for the city of Yeysk. The alert remained active until 5:33 am, lasting roughly three hours.
Ukraine’s General Staff subsequently confirmed that the Yeysk military airfield had been hit and that a fire broke out on the site.
The Russian military uses Yeysk to support aviation operations, including aircraft capable of launching missiles and guided aerial bombs against Ukraine.
The base also hosts Russia’s 859th Center for Combat Application and Retraining of Naval Aviation Flight Personnel, making it an important training and support facility for Russian naval aviation.
Another distinctive feature of Yeysk is its NITKA ground-based aviation training complex, which replicates an aircraft carrier’s flight deck and landing systems. Russian naval aviators use the facility to practice carrier takeoffs and landings without operating at sea.
Repeated Ukrainian attacks have made Yeysk increasingly vulnerable, and Russian forces do not appear to station combat aircraft there permanently. However, aircraft can still be temporarily redeployed to the base ahead of operations.
Ukraine simultaneously struck a Russian drone operations facility in Millerovo, roughly 170 kilometers, or 105 miles, from the front line.
The General Staff said the target was used for the storage, preparation, and launch of Russian attack UAVs. A fire was recorded following the strike.
NASA FIRMS detected a fire in the Millerovo area at approximately 3:33 am local time after drone warnings were issued shortly after midnight.
The Millerovo military airfield is associated with Russia’s 31st Fighter Aviation Regiment, which operates Su-30SM multirole fighters.
The site has repeatedly come under Ukrainian attack because of its proximity to Ukraine and its role in supporting Russian military aviation and drone operations.
Russian forces also use infrastructure in the area to store ammunition, house personnel and maintain fuel and lubricant supplies.
Rostov regional governor Yuri Slyusar acknowledged a drone attack on Millerovo but did not publicly mention the military facility or the fire there.
Previously, Ukrainian drones struck a Russian Nebo-U radar station at the Millerovo military airfield in Russia’s Rostov region, a facility used to launch Shahed drones and other UAVs against Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukraine Hits Russia’s Refineries So Bad Moscow Is Now Importing Fuel for Its Warplanes

Ukraine Hits Russia’s Refineries So Bad Moscow Is Now Importing Fuel for Its Warplanes
Systematic Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries have sharply reduced the country’s aviation fuel production, forcing Moscow to import Jet A-1 from South Korea and Egypt to support both military and civilian aviation, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence said on August 29.
According to HUR, Russia has also temporarily banned exports of its own aviation fuel as it attempts to preserve domestic supplies.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“To meet the needs of combat and civilian aviation, Russia, which for decades positioned itself as an energy superpower, has officially introduced a temporary ban on exports of its own aviation fuel and is forced to seek ways to import foreign Jet A-1 aviation fuel,” Ukrainian intelligence said.
Jet A-1 is broadly comparable to the Soviet- and Russian-standard TS-1 and RT kerosene fuels used in gas-turbine aircraft engines, allowing it to be used by a wide range of aircraft operated by the Russian military.
HUR said the imported fuel is suitable for aircraft including the MiG-29, Su-34, Su-35S, Su-30SM, Su-57 and Su-24M, as well as Tu-95MS strategic bombers.
The fuel could also be used by Russia’s newer jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 attack drones, which employ Telefly TJ2000A turbojet engines or Russian-made equivalents designated TRD-2000.
Ukrainian intelligence said three tankers linked to Russia’s shadow fleet have already delivered approximately 70,000 metric tons of Jet A-1 from South Korea and Egypt to Russian ports in St. Petersburg and Vladivostok.
The shipments were reportedly arranged for Russia’s Independent Oil and Gas Company, which supplies large quantities of fuel to TZK-AERO.
TZK-AERO, in turn, provides fuel under government contracts to the Russian military, the Federal Security Service and other Russian security formations, according to HUR.
Ukrainian intelligence said the supply chain for South Korean aviation fuel involved UAE-based Caliph Energy Trading FZE.
The Egyptian supply route reportedly involved the Middle East Oil Refinery, known as MIDOR, the Egyptian General Petroleum Corporation and UAE-based trading company Vernal Overseas FZE.
Earlier, reports emerged that Russia was considering easing aviation fuel standards in an effort to increase production following Ukrainian strikes on the country’s oil refineries.
Russia’s Transport Ministry has proposed allowing aviation fuel with a freezing point of up to minus 50 degrees Celsius, compared with the current requirement of minus 60 degrees Celsius.

articles.title: Iraq committed to full US withdrawal deadline – media
articles.body:
Iraq committed to full US withdrawal deadline – media
Iraq is committed to a full withdrawal of US-led coalition forces by the end of September, UK-based Saudi daily Asharq Al-Awsat reported on Saturday, citing an Iraqi official.
US forces have been in the country for 23 years since the 2003 invasion and subsequent smaller-scale operations against Islamic State (IS, formerly ISIS).
Reports that US and other foreign troops could remain after September “contradict what was agreed upon between the previous Iraqi government and the US administration,” Asharq Al-Awsat cited the official as saying.
The comments followed media reports suggesting that Washington was only planning a drawdown, rather than a full withdraw by the end of the September deadline.
“This is a transition of the Coalition’s military mission to a more traditional bilateral security partnership,” Iraqi news outlet Shafaq News reported, citing an anonymous US official.
Earlier this month, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s office stated that the September 30 deadline would be “the fixed and final date” for the pullout of international coalition forces.
US President Donald Trump has previously backed reducing the US military presence in Iraq, reaffirming a withdrawal plan originally agreed in 2024 under the Biden administration. During a meeting with al-Zaidi this summer, Trump said the two countries were developing a relationship “where we don’t need the military” in Iraq.
Washington’s presence in the region has taken a significant hit during the Iran war, as Tehran has damaged or outright destroyed key US radar, communications, and other military infrastructure at bases in Gulf nations.
During the conflict, US military infrastructure in the region also faced attacks by pro-Iranian armed groups in Iraq operating outside Baghdad’s direct control.
The Pentagon is now considering whether to reduce the US military footprint in the Gulf after the Iran war ends, The Washington Post reported earlier in August, citing anonymous officials.
US allies in the Gulf have also reportedly expressed frustration over what they see as a lack of proper consultation before the US-Israeli attack on Iran, which led to bases on their territories being targeted. Regional powers have since moved to diversify their security partnerships, with Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan signing the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, already dubbed by commentators an ‘Islamic NATO,’ early this month.

articles.title: Putin, Xi set for Central Asia summit as Russia and China seek to counter Western influence
articles.body:
Putin, Xi set for Central Asia summit as Russia and China seek to counter Western influence
Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping are due in Kyrgyzstan on Monday for a two-day summit, joined by the leaders of Iran and India. The gathering comes as the group seeks to project a united front amid wars in Ukraine and Iran and growing tensions with the West.
Russia's Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping are expected in Central Asia's Kyrgyzstan Monday for a two-day summit, also attended by Iran's and India's leaders, of a regional bloc seeking to be a counter-influence to the West.
Around a dozen heads of states will head to the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek to mark 25 years of the Shanghai Cooperation Group (SCO).
The group brings together Russia, China, India, Pakistan, Iran, four Central Asian countries and Moscow-allied Belarus.
Putin and Xi have previously used SCO summits to promote their vision of a multipolar world and present a united front against the West.
It takes place four-and-a-half years into Moscow's Ukraine invasion and six months into the war between Washington and Tehran. Iran will be represented by its president, Masoud Pezeshkian.
Putin, Xi, Pezeshkian as well as India's Narendra Modi and Pakistan's Shehbaz Sharif are due to take part in a plenary session chaired by Kyrgyz leader Sadyr Japarov.
Read moreXi hosts Putin and Modi at SCO summit in show of Global South unity
Putin is also expected to hold separate bilateral talks with Iran's Pezeshkian and China's Xi, among other leaders, Kremlin spokesman Yuri Ushakov said.
Russia and Iran – among the most sanctioned states in the world – have massively deepened their military and economic ties during the Ukraine war.
US President Donald Trump has warned Moscow and Beijing against arming Iran.
Putin's meeting with Pezeshkian comes days after the CIA's director John Ratcliffe made a rare trip to Moscow, with US media speculating he could have discussed Ukraine and Iran with his Russian counterparts.
The SCO has historically focused on economic issues. It gained momentum in recent years under Moscow's and Beijing's leadership.
On top of its 10 members, it now has 15 "dialogue partners", including Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Qatar. It also has two observer countries: Afghanistan and Mongolia.
The SCO's founding declaration says the group is "not an alliance directed against other states".
Read morePutin seeks to reinforce China ties after Trump-Xi summit
But Putin and Xi have repeatedly made anti-Western speeches during its summits.
At last year's gathering, Putin accused Western countries of provoking the Ukraine war, while Xi denounced "acts of intimidation", referring to US-Chinese tensions.
Real and trade wars
The Bishkek summit takes place as some SCO members are in the midst of real wars – the Ukraine and Iran conflicts – or trade wars, with the imposition of US tariffs on Chinese and Indian goods.
This month, the US slapped secondary sanctions on Iran's trading partners in the sectors of gold, technology, digital assets, aviation, and maritime transport, aiming to cripple the Iranian regime.
Washington also threatened Iran's allies with sanctions.
China, a major importer of Iranian oil, responded by saying it will "firmly defend" its interests.
Iran, living under sanctions since its 1979 revolution ended with Islamic authorities taking charge, has regularly said it will not cave to economic pressure.
But Pezeshkian has acknowledged his country faces "economic difficulties".
Iran only joined the bloc in 2023.
Read moreChina summit a symbol of a world aiming to 'make itself America-proof', expert says
Mohammad Hassan Najmi, an international relations expert, told AFP that Tehran "believes its membership and active participation in these alliances can enable it to circumvent US and European sanctions".
But concrete benefits of the group are uncertain, he said, as "in times of crisis, these alliances have rarely allowed Iran to resolve its difficulties".
While the bloc claims to represent some 40 percent of the world's population and 25 percent of global GDP, it remains diverse, with some disagreements among members.
Russia and China compete for influence in Central Asia – a resource-rich region crucial for the transport of goods between Europe and Asia – while Beijing at times has had strained relations with India and Pakistan.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: US military leaders warn Hegseth over 'unsustainable' Iran war duration: report
articles.body:
Senior US military commanders have warned Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth that the continuing war against Iran is “unsustainable” and threatens the country’s ability to respond to global crises and defend the homeland, The Washington Post reported.
The warnings appeared in the August 14 edition of the Secretary of Defense Orders Book, a classified internal document used to direct military movements.
People familiar with the assessment said the latest edition requires certain personnel currently in the Middle East to remain there through September, while other units have been ordered to continue their deployments into 2027.
The heads of the army, navy and air force, along with four-star commanders responsible for operations in Europe, Asia and Latin America, characterised the six-month war as “too much for too long”.
The leaders of US European Command, US Indo-Pacific Command and US Southern Command, as well as the Navy’s top admiral, formally registered their “non-concurrence” with orders extending the deployment of their forces in the Middle East.
Although the move signals formal disagreement with the defence secretary’s directive, the commanders confirmed that they would still carry out the mission.
The report said the reassignment of ships and surveillance aircraft to US Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, had reduced the military’s capacity for training and homeland defence.
The navy has reportedly stretched its resources to meet wartime demands, raising concerns that insufficient ship maintenance could result in fleet shortages if other conflicts emerge.
Although the Army and Air Force leadership formally concurred with the deployment extensions, they warned that the decision carried “significant risk”.
More than 50,000 US troops are currently stationed in the region.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell declined to discuss the orders book or specific internal disagreements.
He said force allocation decisions were based on “strategic priorities established by the president and the advice of the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and Combatant Commanders”.
It remains unclear when the overstretched units will be allowed to return to their original areas of operation.

articles.title: Taiwan tracks 13 Chinese ships, 3 military aircraft
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of National Defense tracked eight Chinese naval vessels, five official ships, and three military aircraft around Taiwan between 6 a.m. on Saturday and the same time Sunday.
All three of the aircraft crossed the median line and entered the nation’s northern and eastern air defense identification zone, or ADIZ. In response, Taiwan deployed aircraft, naval ships, and coastal-based missile systems to monitor the People’s Liberation Army activity, according to the MND.

articles.title: Putin-Trump-Zelensky summit possible only to 'formalize agreements,' Peskov says

A summit between Russian President Vladimir Putin, U.S. President Donald Trump, and President Volodymyr Zelensky could take place only to formalize agreements already reached, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Aug. 30, according to Russian state-controlled media.
The comments come as peace efforts remain stalled, with Russia continuing to insist on its maximalist conditions and attacking Ukrainian cities.
"Such a meeting is possible only to formalize agreements," Peskov told reporters. He added that a settlement over Ukraine is "not a primitive deal," but a "very complicated" process involving "a huge number of details."
The latest statement follows a recent visit to Moscow by CIA Director John Ratcliffe. Peskov said Ratcliffe met with Russian intelligence officials but did not meet Putin, who was briefed on the discussions. Trump described the Aug. 25 visit as "semi-routine."
Russia has repeatedly rejected or complicated proposals aimed at advancing ceasefire talks. On Aug. 22, Putin said Moscow said he received new proposals for ending the war, calling them "exotic" and "unacceptable."
"The proposals being conveyed to us are sometimes, I would say, exotic in nature and are unacceptable," Putin said. He added that Russia was ready for peace talks only "on the basis of the realities that have developed on the ground," a position he has reiterated throughout the past few years.
The Kremlin has also rejected proposals for a partial aerial ceasefire, while U.S. and Ukrainian officials have explored new approaches to move negotiations forward. Moscow has also rejected other proposals, including an American suggestion to establish a free economic zone in Donbas.

articles.title: Ukraine’s long-term advantage lies in its ability to adapt quickly to changes on battlefield — expert
articles.body:
Ukraine’s long-term advantage lies in its ability to adapt quickly to changes on battlefield — expert
This view was expressed by Can Kasapoğlu, a senior research fellow at the Hudson Institute, in an interview with Ukrinform.
“Three features of Ukraine’s defense technological and industrial base have impressed me. First is adaptive velocity. At occupied Ukrainian Sevastopol, Russia reinforced Soviet-inherited marine-mammal defenses against divers yet failed to anticipate robotic naval attack. Eight months after the full-scale invasion, an early USV struck the heart of the Black Sea Fleet. Apart from its warhead, nothing was military-grade: commercial satellite communications, a jet-ski power pack that one can find and buy online, and a simply workshop-built hull. The same logic drove the FPV revolution—recombining components faster than the enemy adapts,” Kasapoğlu noted.
The expert cited Ukraine’s information architecture as the second key advantage, particularly the Delta system, which, he said, was developed directly in the context of war.
“Fusing commercial LEO imagery, tens of thousands of air, land, and maritime sensors, and acoustic warning networks converts data into information superiority. Russia retains advantages in manpower, industry, and authoritarian partners; Ukraine compensates through a higher-quality picture of the battlespace,” Kasapoğlu emphasized.
The expert identified combat data as the third distinctive feature of the Ukrainian defense sector, noting that it has become a strategic asset.
“Secure data rooms and AI infrastructure turn battlefield experience into military-grade datasets and data into defense diplomacy,” the expert stressed.
In his view, after the war, Ukraine must maintain the mechanism of interaction between the front lines and the defense industry, protect the accumulated combat data sets, diversify the supply of components, and develop long-term joint ventures with allies.
“Ukraine’s enduring advantage is not any single drone, but the ecosystem that learns faster than its adversaries,” Kasapoğlu concluded.
As reported by Ukrinform, Can Kasapoğlu believes that Ukraine is providing NATO countries with invaluable lessons—ranging from the effective use of low-cost technologies on the battlefield to building national resilience and preparing for protracted wars.

articles.title: Israel pounds southern Lebanon as Iran vows to stand by Beirut
