Israel pounds southern Lebanon as Iran vows to stand by Beirut
Israel continued attacks across southern Lebanon on Saturday, carrying out airstrikes, artillery shelling and demolitions, while Tehran pledged continued support for the country amid stalled negotiations over an IDF withdrawal.
Most of the day’s attacks were concentrated in Nabatieh Province, RT’s Lebanon correspondent Steve Sweeney said. Two explosions were reported near Aita al-Jabal, while Israeli drones carried out two strikes on Nabatieh al-Fawqa on Saturday morning. Israeli forces separately set fire to homes in Beit Yahoun.
The latest strikes came two days after an Israeli attack on Arab Salim killed 28-year-old Saja Sharara just 48 hours after her wedding, according to Sweeney, who recently visited the southern Lebanese village. Six others were wounded, including a child, a woman, and two elderly people.
Israel, however, said Thursday’s strikes followed the launch of two Hezbollah drones toward Israeli troops.
The escalation comes as Tehran reaffirms its support for Lebanon. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met Sheikh Ali al-Khatib, vice president of Lebanon’s Higher Shiite Islamic Council, in Tehran on Friday. According to Lebanese L’Orient Today, Khatib described a deteriorating situation in the south, saying many displaced residents had exhausted their savings and had been left without homes or work. He appealed in particular for financial assistance for affected communities.
Araghchi said Tehran was working to revive the US-Iran memorandum of understanding signed in June, the first clause of which called for an end to Israeli attacks on Lebanon. He argued that implementing the agreement remained the way to resolve the crisis, while acknowledging that “the circumstances are difficult,” as cited by L’Orient Today.
The memorandum followed a renewed escalation between Israel and Hezbollah after the latter resumed attacks two days after the US-Iran war began on February 28. Hezbollah said its operation was retaliation for the killing of former Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei.
Hezbollah says it has observed the ceasefire reached under the subsequent US-Iran agreement. Israel, however, has continued strikes and demolitions in southern Lebanon and currently occupies more than 600 square kilometers of Lebanese territory.
Beirut and Israel have meanwhile been holding direct negotiations aimed at securing an Israeli withdrawal and ending the hostilities. Another round is reportedly expected in Rome in September, but progress has been limited.

articles.title: German establishment figures call for ban on country’s most popular party
articles.body:
German establishment figures call for ban on country’s most popular party
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius and Baden-Wurttemberg Governor Cem Ozdemir have called for the opposition Alternative for Germany (AfD) party to be banned. The two establishment politicians claim that the country’s most popular party poses a threat to Germany’s constitutional order and democracy.
The AfD is the largest opposition force in the Bundestag and enjoys the support of 28% of respondents, according to recent surveys.
The right-wing party advocates tougher immigration controls while also calling for an end to Germany’s green policies. It is also highly critical of Berlin’s support for Ukraine and sanctions against Russia.
In an opinion piece published by the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung on Friday, Pistorius and Ozdemir drew parallels between the modern-day AfD and Adolf Hitler’s National Socialist party.
“Today, we are once again facing a threat to democracy from the extreme right,” the politicians, who represent the Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the Green Party, respectively, claimed.
In making their case for outlawing the right-wing party, Pistorius and Ozdemir argued that a powerful faction within the AfD espouses the idea of ‘remigration’, thus calling into question the “inviolability of human dignity” enshrined in the German constitution.
“We cannot confront ethnic nationalist ideology through political debate. That would be naive,” the authors wrote.
“A legal review of the constitutionality of a political party is warranted when it calls into question and threatens the continued existence of our democracy,” Pistorius and Ozdemir stated.
The two also took issue with the AfD’s supposedly “pro-Russian stance,” describing it as a “security risk.” The opposition party’s calls for Germany to withdraw from the European Union, the Eurozone, and NATO are equally “dangerous,” according to the article.
While acknowledging the AfD’s rising popularity, Pistorius and Ozdemir argued that widespread public support for the party is another reason why it should be banned outright.
Voting for the opposition party out of dissatisfaction with the current state of affairs in Germany is no excuse, the authors argued.
“The undeniable radicalization of the AfD makes it impossible to claim ignorance of who one is voting for,” they wrote.
At present, Germany’s domestic intelligence agency classifies the AfD as a ‘suspected right-wing extremist’ entity – a designation that gives the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV) powers to surveil the party and its members. In several regions, local AfD chapters have been subjected to even wider monitoring.
Meanwhile, an INSA poll published by Bild earlier this month showed that support for Germany’s governing Christian Democratic CDU/CSU bloc had fallen to 20%, with some 78% of respondents dissatisfied with Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s coalition government, which also includes the Social Democrats.

articles.title: US military chiefs warn Hegseth that Iran war is weakening forces needed to counter intl. threats
articles.body:
The heads of the US armed forces jointly warned US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth against continuing operations in Iran, The Washington Post reported on Sunday.
According to people familiar with the matter, the heads of the army, navy, and air force, along with the commanders who head the US military’s operations in Europe, Asia, and Latin America, warned Hegseth that continuing the war in Iran risks weakening their ability to confront threats elsewhere around the world.
The warnings were detailed in the August 14 edition of the Secretary of Defense Orders Book (SDOB), which is classified. The people with knowledge spoke on the condition of anonymity.
The SDOB details the worldwide availability of the US’s military assets, such as warships, aircraft, personnel, and weapons systems. It also reflects the president’s priorities for the armed forces, which the defense secretary and the branches of the military carry out.
US military heads disagree with Hegseth orders to keep troops in Middle East until 2027, still will carry it out
The orders book reportedly stated some US troops deployed in the Middle East to remain there through September, while others would remain in the region until 2027, sources familiar with the matter said.
The Washington Post reported that the navy’s top admiral, along with the leaders from America’s European Command, Pacific Command, and the Southern Command, responded with “non-concur,” which means that they do not agree with Hegseth’s order, but will execute it regardless.
Leaders from the US Army and Air Force both noted that the extension of their forces comes with significant risks.
One person familiar with the matter said that US military leadership believes that the war in Iran has been “too much for too long.”
“Decisions regarding the scope and duration of specific force commitments to any Combatant Command are made based on the current threat assessment, strategic priorities established by the President, and the advice of the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and Combatant Commanders,” Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement to the Washington Post.
He added that the Pentagon “does not discuss internal operational processes,” such as the SDOB, “or specific concurrences, non-concurrences, or risk assessments provided by the Services or Combatant Commands during force allocation deliberations.”

articles.title: U.S. Army’s newest tank prototype heads to 1st Cavalry Division
articles.body:
- The U.S. Army's 1st Cavalry Division will test M1E3 Abrams and XM30 prototypes, according to the division's own social media announcement.
- The M1E3 is designed with a hybrid-electric drive, an autoloader and integrated protection in a lighter frame than current Abrams tanks.
The U.S. Army will send its M1E3 Abrams prototype to the 1st Cavalry Division for testing, the division confirmed in a social media post responding to an Army announcement about the next-generation tank.
The 1st Cavalry Division said it will receive both M1E3 prototypes and XM30 prototypes, testing the vehicles and providing feedback that will help shape the Army’s approach to future armored formations.
“And guess who gets to play with them first. The First Team will receive not only the M1E3 prototypes but also the XM30 prototypes to test, provide feedback on and to shape the future of Armored warfare,” the division wrote.
The Army’s announcement described the M1E3 as featuring a hybrid-electric drive, an autoloader and integrated protection systems built into a lighter frame than the current Abrams variants in service.
“The M1E3 Abrams represents a bold step forward in modern vehicle design, combining advanced protection, reduced weight, and a smaller logistical footprint to meet the challenges of tomorrow’s battlefield,” said Michelle Link, Deputy Capability Program Executive for Ground Combat Platforms.
The Army first showed the M1E3 publicly on January 14 at the Detroit Auto Show, presenting it as an early demonstrator built to test unmanned turret architecture, crew layout, digital systems and automation ahead of a planned M1A3 production tank. The design followed the Army’s earlier AbramsX concept demonstrator and reflects lessons the service says it drew from combat losses of donor Abrams tanks in Ukraine, where independent trackers and Ukrainian officials have reported significant losses among the 31 M1A1 tanks delivered, with estimates varying by source.
The most significant change from earlier Abrams variants is the unmanned turret. All three crew members, the commander, gunner and driver, are relocated into an armored crew capsule in the forward hull rather than sitting inside the turret itself, removing them from the tank’s most exposed section.
For targeting, the M1E3 uses the Leonardo DRS Stabilized Sight System, known as S3, as the commander’s panoramic sight, replacing the Safran PASEO system used on the earlier AbramsX demonstrator. The S3 is available in long-wave and mid-wave infrared variants and is also used on the Army’s M-LIDS counter-drone system.
Secondary armament comes from an EOS R400 Mk2 remote weapon station mounted atop the turret. In its displayed configuration, the station combines a 40mm Mk19 automatic grenade launcher, a 7.62mm machine gun and a launcher holding a single FGM-148 Javelin anti-tank missile. The R400 Mk2 is paired with an EchoGuard radar system for detecting and tracking small drones, giving the tank a built-in counter-UAS capability. Army representatives have said the weapon station’s loadout is modular and can be reconfigured depending on mission needs.
The Army has described the overall approach as built around a Modular Open Systems Architecture, intended to let new sensors, weapons and electronic warfare systems be added later through standardized interfaces rather than requiring a full redesign.
The Army has said four early M1E3 prototypes are planned, intended for testing with operational units to evaluate how the new features perform in practice, with serial production targeted for the end of the decade.
Separately, the XM30 program aims to replace the Bradley Infantry Fighting Vehicle, with General Dynamics Land Systems and American Rheinmetall Vehicles competing as finalists. General Dynamics delivered its XM30 Wolf prototype to the Army at Aberdeen Proving Ground last week.
The Army has not disclosed a specific delivery date for the M1E3 prototypes to the 1st Cavalry Division, based at Fort Cavazos, Texas, the total number of prototypes involved in this testing phase, or a timeline for when soldier feedback will inform further development of the design.

articles.title: Ukraine offers invaluable lessons to NATO, from new technologies to national resilience – expert
articles.body:
Ukraine offers invaluable lessons to NATO, from new technologies to national resilience – expert
Can Kasapoğlu, Senior Fellow and Defense Analyst at Hudson Institute, said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
“Ukraine offers invaluable lessons to NATO. The first one is pennies versus dollars. Affordable, scalable, sustainable mass can outperform exquisite systems in combat,” Kasapoğlu said.
According to the expert, comparing the cost of Ukrainian drones with the value of the Russian equipment they destroy showed how defense-economics asymmetry can systematically impose attrition.
In his view, the second important lesson is the need to assess “red lines” rather than mythologize them.
“Ukraine sank the Moskva, struck Moscow, attacked Crimea and Alabuga, damaged energy infrastructure, and hit strategic-bomber bases through Operation Spiderweb. Before the war, Western analyses portrayed such actions as possible thresholds for Russian tactical nuclear use. That escalation did not occur. The risk remains, but deterrence requires empirical judgment, not paralysis,” Kasapoğlu said.
The expert identified national resilience as the third lesson.
“Few expected Ukraine to withstand a war of this scale, making national resilience-building as important as weapons procurement,” he stressed.
In addition, Kasapoğlu said, NATO must prepare for protracted interstate wars.
As reported by Ukrinform, peace requires pressure on every member of the coalition supporting Russia until continuing the war forces them into a serious dilemma and a settlement begins to offer them benefits.

articles.title: PLA shift to systems warfare means Taiwan’s defences need to change: experts
articles.body:
PLA shift to systems warfare means Taiwan’s defences need to change: experts
Conflicts in Ukraine and Iran have shown the power of integration and the extension of targets to include critical civilian infrastructure
Instead of focusing on individual weapons, the PLA has progressively emphasised integrating intelligence, AI, communications, weapons, logistics and infrastructure into an overall combat system, they warn.
“The PLA is no longer concerned only with whose weapons are stronger, but with who can connect different weapons to generate greater overall combat power,” said Chen Chia-sheng, a researcher at a government-funded think tank in Taipei.
In an article published last week by his organisation, the Institute for National Defence and Security Research, Chen wrote that for Taiwan, this meant the threat in a cross-strait conflict could extend well beyond attacks on its fighters, warships and missile batteries.
Under what the PLA calls “systems destruction warfare”, Beijing could seek to disable critical nodes supporting Taiwanese forces, including satellites, radar, communications links, command centres, data networks and fuel and logistics facilities, he wrote.
Once those links were severed, even sophisticated weapons could rapidly lose their effectiveness without being physically destroyed, he added.

articles.title: Mapping the Iran war’s strikes on Gulf energy – and what comes next for oil
articles.body:
Mapping Iran war’s strikes on Gulf energy and its impact on future of oil
US energy companies have reaped billions from rising oil price, but their assets in the region remain at risk.
Six months into the war on Iran, the largest US oil companies have posted their biggest profits since 2022, selling less oil at far higher prices. But the conflict is also putting their longstanding Gulf investments at risk, exposing the industry’s uneasy balance between wartime gains and mounting geopolitical vulnerability for investors worldwide.
Since the war began on February 28, Brent crude has risen about 22 percent, from $72 to $88 a barrel.
The Strait of Hormuz – through which one-fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas was shipped before the war – remains largely closed to commercial traffic, though Iran and Oman agreed last week on a temporary maritime route. Iran says the strait will not fully reopen until the United States fulfils its commitments under a lapsed interim peace deal, leaving longer-term security and management arrangements unresolved.
In the absence of a lasting resolution, the disruption is likely to continue supporting higher energy prices and creating windfalls for producers, despite placing energy companies’ regional assets and future projects at greater risk.
Rahul Choudhary, vice president of Upstream Research at Rystad Energy, an independent energy research company, said the conflict has already reduced the amount of oil and gas US energy firms are drawing from the Gulf region.
“Overall we expect US companies’ share of gas supplies [from the region] to fall by around 40 percent this year compared to last year [and] the share of oil supplies to drop by 30-35 percent,” he told Al Jazeera.
While higher commodity prices have helped offset the immediate financial impact, Choudhary said prolonged disruption is likely to delay major projects and weigh on the future growth plans of US oil and gas companies with a presence in the region.
Who has profited?
The surge in the oil price since early March, when Iran first closed the Strait of Hormuz, has delivered a windfall for oil companies, but gains have been tempered by challenges in the Gulf.
Chevron has limited exposure to Arab Gulf supply disruptions, with the region accounting for just 5 percent of its total global output. The group reported its highest quarterly profit in six years of $12bn in adjusted earnings on July 31.
ExxonMobil, by contrast, has been far more exposed to disruption in the Middle East, with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and Iranian attacks on US-linked infrastructure in the region affecting its operations in Qatar and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), which together account for 20 percent of its global equity upstream supply, according to Choudhary.
“We already saw in H1 [the first half of] 2026, the company’s upstream earnings dropped by around $1.3bn compared to H1 2025, due to lower upstream volumes from the Middle East. However, the shortfall was covered well by higher commodity prices,” Choudhary said.
The contrast highlights a broader divide between those US energy companies which have benefitted from tighter global supply – and the corresponding rise in the oil price – and those with assets, partnerships or operations in the Gulf at greater risk of disruption caused by recent attacks on energy facilities.
Where are US energy companies exposed in the Gulf?
The Gulf’s energy sector is dominated by state-owned giants such as Saudi Aramco, Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) and QatarEnergy.
Although these national oil and gas companies retain control over the region’s reserves and core infrastructure, US energy firms have carved out strategic positions across the region.
US companies generate revenue through stakes in production assets, joint ventures, production agreements, refining and petrochemical projects, as well as through long-term contracts to provide equipment, engineering and operational expertise.
ExxonMobil has some of the largest US commercial interests in the Gulf.
The company has been a major partner in Qatar’s LNG sector for decades, holding stakes in several QatarEnergy LNG joint ventures linked to the expansion of the North Field. The field is the Qatari section of the North Field-South Pars structure, the world’s largest natural gas field, which Qatar shares with Iran, where it is known as South Pars. ExxonMobil also holds an interest in the UAE’s Upper Zakum offshore oilfield alongside ADNOC.
Similarly, ConocoPhillips joined the North Field East (NFE) and North Field South (NFS) expansion projects with QatarEnergy in 2022 to increase export capacity at Ras Laffan.
The US group, Occidental Petroleum, has become one of the largest foreign producers in Oman, operating the Mukhaizna heavy oilfield, the country’s biggest producing oilfield. It also holds interests in UAE gas and pipeline projects.
Chevron maintains a smaller but strategically important Gulf footprint. Through Saudi Arabian Chevron, the company operates oil assets in the Saudi-Kuwait Partitioned Zone, including the Wafra field. In July, it said it was exploring potential routes to move Iraqi crude to Mediterranean export terminals, which could reduce reliance on the Strait of Hormuz.
Where have attacks on energy facilities taken place?
According to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED), a US-registered independent conflict monitor, Iran and Iran-backed groups in the region have carried out at least 172 attacks on nonmilitary infrastructure across the six Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries since the US and Israel launched their war on February 28.
Energy infrastructure has been hit hardest, with oil and gas facilities, along with power plants and desalination plants, accounting for nearly half (48 percent) of all strikes on nonmilitary targets.
The UAE, Kuwait and Bahrain have suffered the highest number of successful strikes, with the majority aimed at oil and gas facilities.
Among the sites that have been struck are Kuwait’s Mina Abdullah and Mina al-Ahmadi refineries, the Bahrain Petroleum Company oil refinery, and ADNOC’s al-Ruwais Industrial City and the Habshan gas complex.
There have also been several strikes on Saudi Aramco facilities, most recently a drone strike on July 27 on the Abqaiq processing complex, one of the most critical nodes in Saudi Arabia’s oil infrastructure, processing more than seven million barrels of oil per day.
Nasser Khdour, Middle East assistant research manager at ACLED, said: “Oil and gas facilities, power plants and water desalination plants are likely to remain key targets for Iran because disruption to these sectors can increase economic pressure on Gulf states, while disruption to global energy supplies increases prices and pressure on the US during periods of escalation.”
In March, a drone attack close to the Saudi Aramco-ExxonMobil SAMREF refinery in Yanbu disrupted oil loading at the city’s Red Sea port. While the attack had only minimal operational impact, it highlighted the vulnerability of US-linked energy assets in the region.
Qatar’s Ras Laffan Industrial City, the world’s largest LNG export hub, which hosts major joint ventures between QatarEnergy, ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips, also came under repeated attack in March, at one point forcing the plant to halt production entirely. In June, an explosion as a result of a “technical malfunction” on Qatar’s Barzan gas project, where ExxonMobil holds a stake, killed at least 13 people.
“In terms of gas assets being impacted, major blows have been [dealt to] companies [that are] part of LNG projects in Qatar: ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips,” Choudhary said.
He added that ExxonMobil’s share of LNG supply from Qatar is expected to fall significantly this year to about four million tonnes compared with 13 million tonnes last year, while ConocoPhillips has also experienced reduced volumes to one million tonnes this year compared with 2.5 million tonnes last year.
The attacks on Qatar’s LNG infrastructure could have longer-term consequences. Damage to LNG trains at Ras Laffan could take years to repair, according to QatarEnergy, while delays to Qatar’s North Field expansion projects could push back planned supply growth.
“The attack on LNG trains 4 and 6 at Rasgas damaged roughly 13 million tonnes of capacity, which will take anywhere between three to five years to come back online with a total repair cost estimate of around $3bn,” said Choudhary.
He added that the second most impacted gas project has been the Shah gas project in the UAE, in which Occidental Petroleum has a 40-percent stake and where drone attacks in March caused a fire at the gas plant that halted operations.
The conflict has also affected ExxonMobil’s oil interests in the UAE, Choudhary said. Production from Upper Zakum, where ExxonMobil has a 28 percent stake, was reduced between March and May when export routes were disrupted, limiting the ability to move offshore crude.
Beyond the UAE, the most significant impact on US companies’ oilfield operations played out in Iraq. A drone attack hit the Sarsang oilfield in March, followed by an explosion at one of its storage facilities in April, together causing damage to the field.
Looking ahead, Choudhary said higher prices could support cash flows, but prolonged conflict risks could threaten future growth. ExxonMobil’s $10bn Upper Zakum and Qatar LNG expansions could face delays, while ConocoPhillips remains exposed through investments in higher-risk markets, including its planned 42-percent stake in BP’s Kirkuk operations in Iraq.
“For companies like Chevron and Occidental Petroleum, whose presence are in less volatile countries like Israel and Oman respectively, the impact of escalations will not be as severe, as we have not seen significant disruption in these countries,” said Choudhary.
US oilfield service companies in the Gulf
Oilfield service giants, including US firms SLB (formerly Schlumberger), Halliburton and Baker Hughes, provide drilling technologies, equipment and operational expertise across the Gulf, supporting Saudi Aramco, ADNOC and QatarEnergy.
For oilfield service companies, the outlook is mixed, according to Chinmayi Teggi, energy research analyst at Rystad Energy, a research group. While higher oil prices and energy security concerns could lift demand over time, near-term margins remain under pressure from higher logistical costs, supply-chain disruptions and delayed projects.
“For the Big Three (SLB, Baker Hughes and Halliburton), the conflict continues to weigh on regional revenues,” Teggi told Al Jazeera, adding that second-quarter Middle East revenues were down 8-10 percent compared with the previous year across the three companies, while higher oil prices meant revenues were higher in other geographies.
However, a recovery in suspended operations and production could help drive growth into 2027.
For US companies, therefore, the Gulf remains both an opportunity and a risk.
“The impact on US companies will depend on the extent of exposure and countries in which these companies are present,” Choudhary said.
Their investments have secured US access to some of the world’s most important oil and LNG projects, but the conflict has exposed the risk of operating in a region where energy infrastructure has become increasingly vulnerable to geopolitical conflict.
US President Donald Trump has repeatedly warned Iran against restricting access to the Strait of Hormuz, arguing that the waterway must remain open to global commerce.
But for companies with billions of dollars invested across the Gulf, the challenge isn’t just about keeping shipments moving – it is ensuring the infrastructure remains secure, they say.

articles.title: Russia could have used nukes in Ukraine but chose restraint – top MP
articles.body:
Russia could have used nukes in Ukraine but chose restraint – top MP
Russia could have long ago used tactical nuclear weaponry to achieve victory against Ukraine, but it has always sought to minimize collateral damage, Leonid Slutsky, the head of Russia’s Liberal-Democratic Party (LDPR), has said.
The senior MP, who chairs the Russian State Duma International Affairs Committee, made the remarks in an interview with conservative American journalist and podcaster Tucker Carlson that aired on Saturday. Slutsky said Moscow would only opt for nuclear weaponry against Kiev if its Western sponsors supplied Ukraine with weapons of mass destruction. The politician expressed hope that the situation would not deteriorate to that point.
In any other scenario, use of nuclear weaponry against Ukraine would not fit Moscow’s approach and vision, the MP stated.
“We could have used them long ago and achieved victory, but we always rely on common sense and the principle of minimizing civilian casualties. Using such weapons as an instrument of terror, as was the case in Hiroshima and Nagasaki, if we recall World War II, is alien to us,” Slutsky stated.
Moscow could also have begun hitting Ukraine without any regard for collateral damage and civilian casualties, but still hopes that Kiev and its Western backers will show some “common sense” and come to the “position of peace, not war,” the politician believes.
“But for now they take an entirely different position, completely devoid of common sense,” Slutsky said.
Russia has so far avoided attacking bridges across the Dnieper River, the destruction of which would have deprived the Ukrainian military in Donbass of logistics, the politician explained. He said it has also refrained from striking the key airport of Borispol outside Kiev, which has been used to funnel weaponry from the West. Either option, however, would have drastically worsened the humanitarian situation in Ukraine and harmed civilians, according to Slutsky.

articles.title: In the autumn, the rate of downing Russian drones must be brought above 90% — Zelenskyy

In the autumn, the rate of downing Russian drones must be brought above 90% — Zelenskyy

Over four days, Russia launched nearly 1,500 drones, around 800 of them jet-powered. Ukraine is strengthening its air defense and developing interceptor drones.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy called on the Ministry of Defense and the military to maximize efforts to strengthen capabilities to counter Russian drones, so that by autumn the rate of their destruction exceeds 90%. The head of state reported this on Telegram, UNN writes.

In the Mykolaiv district, the Russians struck a food processing plant with “Shahed” drones yesterday. A warehouse was damaged. There were no casualties.
Also over the past 24 hours, the invaders attacked the Ochakiv, Kutsurub, and Halytsyniv communities with FPV drones. An administrative building was damaged in the village of Solonchaky. There were no casualties.
As reported by Ukrinform, three people were killed and 17 others were wounded in the Kherson region over the past 24 hours as a result of enemy attacks.
Photo: State Emergency Service

articles.title: Ankara summons Ukraine envoy after Black Sea attacks
articles.body:
A Ukrainian drone strikes a Turkish-owned roll-on/roll-off (ro-ro) cargo ship near Russia’s Black Sea port of Novorossiysk earlier this month.
Türkiye summoned Ukraine’s ambassador on Aug. 29 after two Turkish-operated commercial vessels were damaged in separate drone attacks in the Black Sea near the Russian port of Tuapse, according to Turkish Foreign Ministry sources.
Ukrainian Ambassador Naryman Dzhelialov was called to the Foreign Ministry in Ankara after the attacks on the Lider Bordo Mavi and Lider Kocatepe vessels, the sources said.
The Lider Bordo Mavi was struck Aug. 26 while sailing near Tuapse, according to Turkish shipping and regional sources. The vessel, which was carrying fresh produce, caught fire after being hit by three drones, injuring five crew members.
The ship flies the Cameroon flag and is operated by a Turkish company. It had departed from the Turkish Black Sea port of Samsun around Aug. 25 and was headed for Tuapse after reportedly being unable to call at the Russian port of Novorossiysk.
The Lider Kocatepe was sent to the area the following day to assist the damaged vessel but was itself targeted by a drone while en route, according to media reports. It sustained material damage and returned to Samsun.
Ukraine did not immediately publicly claim responsibility for either attack. Russia has attributed similar recent strikes on commercial shipping to Ukrainian forces.
The incidents have heightened concerns over the safety of commercial vessels operating in the Black Sea, where civilian shipping has increasingly been exposed to the effects of the war between Russia and Ukraine.
During the meeting, Turkish officials conveyed Ankara’s concerns over the attacks and stressed the need to protect lives, property, navigation and the marine environment, the ministry sources said.
Türkiye has repeatedly warned that the war should not further threaten civilian maritime traffic or disrupt commercial navigation in the Black Sea. Türkiye has sought to maintain relations with both Russia and Ukraine while positioning itself as a mediator in efforts to limit the war’s impact on civilian and commercial activity.
The full extent of the damage to both vessels was still being assessed on Aug. 31.

articles.title: Chinese fighter jet based on Israeli design sold to Muslim-majority Uzbekistan
articles.body:
Another Muslim country is receiving the legacy of a previous Israeli aircraft project as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu instructs the defense establishment to prepare for the development of a new Israeli fighter jet in an effort to maintain Israel’s defense independence.
A video broadcast on Uzbek television confirmed that Uzbekistan will become the second customer of China’s J-10C fighter jet, after Pakistan became the first country to purchase the aircraft.
The J-10 bears a strong resemblance to Israel’s Lavi fighter jet, developed by Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI), whose production was canceled after a government decision in 1988.
According to foreign reports, China later bought the Lavi's plans to accelerate the development of a domestically produced fourth-generation fighter jet and modernize its air force. The funds China paid helped cover the costs of ending the project in Israel.
The Chinese fighter has already been used in combat, participating in aerial clashes between Pakistan and India last year. The aircraft was reportedly used to shoot down Indian Air Force Rafale fighter jets while carrying the advanced PL-15 radar-guided missile.
Uzbekistan's order reflects increasing Chinese influence in Central Asia
Uzbekistan has ordered 24 J-10 aircraft in the export configuration, a move that reflects China’s growing influence in Central Asia, where countries were previously under Russian influence.
The aircraft, which originated in Lod, is now serving a second Muslim country, although one that maintains diplomatic relations with Israel.
According to assessments, Muslim-majority Bangladesh could also become the next customer for the J-10. The aircraft is cheaper than the American F-16 and is marketed to countries that are not interested in purchasing US-made fighter jets.

articles.title: Russian forces attack port infrastructure in Mykolaiv
articles.body:
Russian forces attack port infrastructure in Mykolaiv

articles.title: Ukraine develops stationary EW and SIGINT system for detecting and jamming FPV drones
articles.body:
Ukraine develops stationary EW and SIGINT system for detecting and jamming FPV drones
Ukrainian defence company Rebel Group has developed a stationary electronic warfare and signals intelligence system called Brama. The company plans to have it codified for use by Ukraine's Defence Forces.
Source: Rebel Group press service
Details: The system combines electronic warfare and signals intelligence functions and is designed to counter FPV drones.
"The system can detect the frequency of analogue video and decode it, and then jam both the video channel and the drone's control channel using directed electronic warfare," the press service said.
When the Brama operator receives data on a target and detects it, they can immediately jam it without any additional equipment. Rebel Group also said that the system has undergone range and laboratory testing.
The Ukrainian company is undergoing the codification procedure in order to have the system approved for use by the defence forces.
Rebel Group is a technology company specialising in development and production of electronic warfare and signals intelligence systems. Some of its systems have been codified and tested at General Staff ranges.
Background:
- Ukrainian company InLab previously presented the Stryi electronic warfare station, designed to counter FPV drones and other unmanned aerial vehicles.
- Defence company Unwave also conducted its first testing of its own electronic warfare systems abroad, showcasing the systems in Czechia.

articles.title: Trump Promises His Venezuela Oil Deal Will Lower Gas Prices. But When?
articles.body:
President Donald Trump announced Friday that the United States has entered a “historic” deal with Venezuela, saying that it gives the U.S. majority control over more than 65 billion barrels of oil reserves. Calling it the “BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY” in a post on Truth Social, he said that the agreement would “substantially lower Gas Prices for all Americans.”
The Trump Administration has long expressed an interest in Venezuela, which boasts the world’s largest proven crude-oil reserves as of 2023—approximately 303 billion barrels, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA).
But the President did not outline how soon, exactly, Americans can expect to feel relief at the pumps. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment on the expected timeline.
The answer is especially relevant amid the ongoing war with Iran. One of the linchpins of the conflict is a Tehran-imposed blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of the world’s oil had previously passed. The move has been consequential for the global economy. In the United States, the national average cost for a gallon of gas is $4.08 as of Saturday, according to the AAA, as compared to $3.20 one year ago.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the deal a “huge win” for America in a social media post on Friday, saying that it means “lowering gas prices here at home.”
Any eventual decline in gas prices could provide relief at a time when Americans are already contending with persistent inflation, which was the focus of remarks made by Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh at the Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium in Wyoming on Friday.
However, it could be a while before the impact of the new deal with Venezuela is directly felt.
What we know about Trump’s Venezuela oil deal
Much of what is known about the deal comes from a statement released on Telegram by acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez late Friday.
“It provides for the development of 17 strategic fields, with a proven potential of 65 billion barrels of oil, more than $100 billion in investment and more than $209 billion in tax revenue for the state,” the statement said. “These investments will contribute not only to the recovery and modernization of our industry, but also to our country’s economic growth, the energy security of our hemisphere and greater stability in international markets.”
Despite its vast oil reserves, the country only produced about 1.1 million barrels per day in July, according to a secondary-source estimate from the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries.
The EIA has attributed Venezuela’s long-term production decline largely to “government mismanagement, international sanctions, and the country’s economic crisis,” which contributed to “a lack of investment and maintenance in the energy sector and a deteriorating infrastructure.” The agency found that Venezuela’s total energy production declined by an average of 8.2% annually between 2011 and 2021.
“The U.S. deal with Venezuela is very important strategically,” says Claudio Galimberti, the chief economist at Rystad Energy. “The new wave of investments that is about to come to Venezuela as a result of this deal will be crucial to turn around the country's aging oil infrastructure. Venezuela will be able to increase its production at a faster rate and unlock barrels that would otherwise have stayed underground.”
The agreement envisions private operators playing a central role in that effort. Rodríguez’s post explained that the agreement allows Venezuela to increase its oil production “through the participation of private operators,” without further elaboration.
A State Department official tells TIME that Rodríguez has granted a private company, which is “a joint project of the U.S. government and an experienced private operator in Venezuela,” 100-year rights to develop the fields, adding: “This new entity will be the second largest corporate holder of proven reserves after Saudi Aramco.”
The deal would give the U.S. 55% of the new company’s effective output, “split between equity ownership and guaranteed at-cost off-take,” the official says.
Although they declined to comment on the expected timeline for these steps, the official adds: "As the company scales production, the resulting stable supply of at-cost oil in our Hemisphere will go toward filling the U.S. strategic petroleum reserve and fulfilling the supply needs of our Great U.S. Military.”
Other key factors also remain unknown—including how the deal will be financed and whether it includes any target dates for achieving various outcomes.
Why gas prices won’t lower immediately
One of the main reasons that Americans are unlikely to see immediate relief from high gas prices is that the deal is linked to 17 oil fields in Venezuela, not access to 65 billion barrels of already-produced crude oil.
While those fields contain proven reserves, Venezuela does not have the infrastructure in place currently to produce the oil at a rate that would significantly and rapidly affect the wallets of everyday Americans.
Such concerns arose after former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro was ousted by the United States in January, when oil executives and analysts assessed the viability of developing the country’s reserves.
Speaking at the White House on Jan. 9, ExxonMobil Chairman and CEO Darren Woods called it “uninvestable,” given his assessment of the “legal and commercial constructs—frameworks—in place today in Venezuela.”
“There's an opportunity in Venezuela with all the resources there,” he said. “We don't have that challenge of finding; we have the challenge of developing those resources.”
Patrick De Haan, the head of petroleum analysis for GasBuddy/PDI, provides a similar assessment. He tells TIME, “While the hope of lower gas prices sounds promising, it still will take billions of investment to get that oil.”
In her statement, Rodríguez said the initiative is expected to “facilitate a significant flow of investment aimed at the recovery and reconstruction of strategic infrastructure for the development of our hydrocarbons industry.”
But it remains unclear where that investment will come from, including whether the private operator will provide the financing and how the project will proceed “at no cost to the American Taxpayer,” as Trump said.
De Haan also questioned whether the agreement’s unusual structure could discourage investment. “How can the U.S. lay claim to a sovereign country’s natural resources?” he says, adding that even with approval from Venezuela’s acting president, a 100-year contract could face legal challenges or prove difficult to enforce.
“That may slow down oil companies from wanting to invest in Venezuela,” he explains.
And financing is only one hurdle; the physical work required also shapes the timeline.
“Drilling and pumping that oil will take a very long time. Changes to fuel prices won’t happen overnight or even in months,” De Haan says, adding that global refining capacity is currently constrained, further limiting the speed at which additional crude supply could affect the market.
Galimberti says that consumers should expect a long road between the initial investment and the ultimate production and distribution of oil.
“You will need to factor in several quarters and, in quite a few cases, years,” he says. “Therefore, it is a deal whose benefits will be seen mostly in the medium-long term.”
“To lower gasoline and diesel prices in the short term, the most effective way by far is by increasing the flows from the Middle East,” Galimberti says. He points to recent successes in bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, including pipelines and ports being developed across the Gulf.
Even without potential legal hurdles from within Venezuela, executing on the promise of the reserves could take years, which means that Americans may be in for a wait before they see the impact at gas stations across the U.S.

articles.title: AI’s worst disasters will arrive unannounced | Letters
articles.body:
Timothy Garton Ash is right that serious artificial intelligence risks demand international action, but “AI Hiroshima” may be the wrong picture (Would even an AI disaster on the scale of Hiroshima be enough to make humankind protect itself? I fear not, 22 August). Hiroshima was not technology going rogue. Human beings designed the bomb, authorised its use and dropped it. The technology worked much as intended.
AI may one day behave in ways we cannot control, but many of the gravest harms could happen without any dramatic moment when “the AI takes over”. AI might help design a pathogen, find a vulnerability in critical infrastructure or improve a weapons system while people still decide what happens next. Other harms may build almost invisibly through thousands of ordinary decisions – more autonomy here, one safeguard removed there, another consequential task handed over because the system has worked well so far. By the time the danger is obvious, the important decisions may already have been made.
That is also where international agreement could begin. We do not need countries to agree about superintelligence or the probability of human extinction before agreeing that there are some doors AI should never be allowed to open by itself. Weapons systems, critical infrastructure and biological synthesis are obvious places to start. Governments could agree minimum safeguards, require clear human authority for the most consequential actions, keep records of who authorised what and share serious failures and near-misses internationally.
The greatest AI dangers may not arrive with a mushroom cloud. They may arrive quietly, one apparently reasonable step at a time. If we want effective AI governance, we need to fight the right battle, not the most cinematic one.
Dr Simon Nieder
Chesterfield, Derbyshire
Prof Jonathan Michie (Letters, 26 August) reminds us that the Serbelloni group, led by the author’s father, Donald Michie (when he was at Edinburgh University), was weighing the social dangers of artificial intelligence as long ago as 1972. Nor is AI technology itself new, since its roots run back through to Frank Rosenblatt’s perceptron of 1957, to the Dartmouth workshop of 1956, and to Alan Turing before that. What is new is that we now have the hardware and software infrastructures to drive it forward at what can sometimes seem to be a terrifying speed.
The Lighthill report of 1973 duly delivered an AI winter in the UK, and the field’s centre of gravity crossed the Atlantic, with the consequences that we all now live with. Donald Michie had worked alongside Turing at Bletchley Park and argued forcefully against the cuts, in the televised Lighthill debate that followed the report, to no avail. The quip attributed to him, perhaps apocryphally, “Let there be Lighthill. And there was darkness”, still resonates strongly in our country today.
As a double-hatted academic (computer scientist and humanities scholar), I would argue for the return of a “Serbelloni debate” that, as Jonathan Michie observes and as his father recognised, requires the involvement of both the sciences and the humanities.
Dr Anthony Harris
Emmanuel College, Cambridge
In his article about regulating AI (I worked at OpenAI. Here are the guardrails we need now, 21 August), Miles Brundage failed to mention an international effort seeking broad political support for a global AI treaty. This effort is carrying forward a compelling address at the inaugural UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva last month, where the secretary general called for human control of AI as its applications spread in weaponry and subversive, prejudicial public surveillance
A fragmented approach, as described by Mr Brundage, is likely to greatly increase the difficulty of implementing AI controls that are timely, internationally negotiated, and therefore effective.
AI, corporate agendas, diverse national defence and economic goals, and the proliferation of energy-intensive datacentres are entangled in interlocking systemic interrelationships that cannot be resolved through disjointed incrementalism. This is especially true as the pace of innovation accelerates, exacerbating worst-case scenarios of advanced AI technology, posing increasingly dire risks.
No matter how well intended, fragmented efforts will be diversionary and cause crucial delays, impeding the diligent pursuit of a systemic global strategy to pre-empt destructive outcomes. Such outcomes could result from malicious use of AI by humans and/or subversive and deceptive activities of renegade algorithms – examples of which are already alarming.
Another troubling aspect of this systemic dilemma must be addressed. Mounting bipartisan opposition to datacentres – well-justified and well-substantiated – is diverting the political attention needed to control AI and implement appropriate restraints (bans or moratoriums) until reliable AI safeguards can be established. This is analogous to focusing on treating a serious symptom in lieu of urgently seeking a remedy for the critical disease that’s causing it. Surely it’s possible to employ a multifaceted strategy, recognising that the sooner rigorous AI guardrails are established, the fewer datacentre harms will be suffered.
Like climate change, the threats of advanced AI are inherently global, making an international approach essential.
David Kyler
Saint Simons Island, Georgia, US

articles.title: Khamenei calls Gulf States for 'unity among Muslims' in social media statement
articles.body:
Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei released a written statement on Sunday urging Gulf rulers to “identify their real enemy and understand the plans to confront it.”
Khamenei’s message, issued in commemoration of Islam’s Prophet Mohammed, called for “unity among Muslims” and mutual defense against their enemies.
Iran’s leader hasn’t been seen for months since he got caught up in the opening strikes of the last Israel-Iran war, where his father and predecessor, Ali Khamenei, was killed.
According to Israeli and American assessments, Mojtaba Khamenei, though severely wounded, survived the attack and currently rules the country.
“The Muslims’ unity in the face of the world’s disbelief is a Quranic strategy and a basic teaching of the pure Islam of Prophet Mohammed, not a superficial or transient matter,” Khamenei wrote in his statement.
Araghchi pushes for diplomacy
Last Tuesday, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi published a message saying that “Iran’s commitment to peace and stability is matched by steadfast diplomacy with our neighbors.”
The Iranian official has been meeting with several representatives from neighboring nations, notably Oman and Pakistan, in a new push for regional diplomacy.
“In talks with Pakistani and Omani guests, regional solutions were stressed. A proposed framework for a new corridor, joint mine-clearing, and future management of Hormuz is a case in point,” Araghchi wrote.
Later on Friday, the Iranian foreign minister said that he had met Qatar’s foreign minister and that “putting diplomacy back on track isn’t impossible.”
“It hinges on the United States understanding of one simple fact: Pressure doesn’t work. The US should build trust, speak respectfully, acknowledge our rights, and uphold commitments,” Araghchi said.

articles.title: Ukraine defence chief pledges 'clear' war plan to win early loan release
articles.body:
Ukraine defence chief pledges 'clear' war plan to win early loan release
KYIV, Aug 30 - Ukraine's new defence minister pledged a "clear" vision for Kyiv's partners on how his country plans to fight Russia with more resources, in a bid to bring forward part of a European Union loan to help cover a $27 billion military budget deficit.
The Ukrainian government relies heavily on foreign funds to continue its war effort, now in its fifth year, with the EU committing €90 billion in financing through 2027.
In comments to reporters released on Sunday, Yevhenii Khmara said Kyiv would seek to bring forward part of the €45 billion loan planned for next year, as well as lobby allies for greater contributions and new countries that had not yet given.
"Ukraine will present partners with a clear vision and a clear plan: what tasks the Defence Forces face, what projects are needed for this, what results must be achieved, and within what timeframes," he said.
The EU has earmarked €45 billion each for 2026 and 2027, allowing Ukraine to channel record funds toward defence. President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said last week that Kyiv had spent more than expected in the first half of the year.
'COMMON VISION' FOR WAR
Khmara took over as defence minister last month from Mykhailo Fedorov, whose dismissal sparked rare wartime protests that prompted Zelenskiy to also fire his unpopular military chief.
A former special-forces commander credited with leading Ukraine's deep-strike campaign against Russia, Khmara said he shared a "common vision" with new top general Mykhailo Drapatyi.
Kyiv is seeking to seize the initiative from Moscow, partly by stepping up long-range drone strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, defence manufacturing and logistics.
But it faces a critical shortage of manpower and air defences to fend off Russian air attacks on Ukrainian cities. Kyiv's military has also faced controversy over abuses and mismanagement in recruitment and on the battlefield.
Khmara said Ukraine needs "proper decisions" to preserve lives and a clear vision throughout the ranks for how to fight and end the war.
"This vision must be communicated down the chain to commanders and units carrying out missions at the front every day," he said.
Khmara said Ukraine has tested four potential interceptors to shoot down the jet-powered drones Russia is increasingly firing at Ukraine.
Swarms of the high-speed drones have plagued the capital Kyiv for four consecutive days, killing residents, damaging homes and warehouses and upending daily life. REUTERS

articles.title: Finnish citizens outraged by their president’s policy toward Russia — politician
articles.body:
MOSCOW, August 30. /TASS/. Finnish citizens are deeply outraged by President Alexander Stubb’s handling of the country’s foreign policy, especially with regard to Russia, Armando Mema, a member of the Freedom Alliance national conservative party, told TASS.
"Finns are deeply outraged by the president’s handling of Finland’s foreign policy, particularly regarding Russia," he noted. "A serious economic crisis, massive public debt, and rising unemployment are the harsh realities that Finns face daily. The president’s role should be to maintain good relations with everyone on the international stage, especially neighboring countries. However, Finland’s foreign policy is currently dictated by NATO, and Finns have little influence over foreign affairs," the politician pointed out.
Mema emphasized that the direction in which Stubb is leading Finland "remains uncertain and very dangerous."
Stubb had previously stated that Finland would soon need to resume dialogue with Russia, but shortly thereafter he supported Ukraine’s strikes on civilian logistics infrastructure.

articles.title: Finnish president: Ukraine is the best guarantee of our security against Russia
articles.body:
Finnish president: Ukraine is the best guarantee of our security against Russia
Finnish President Alexander Stubb has said Ukraine is now "in a stronger and better position than at any other point during this war" and is "the best guarantee of security against Russia".
Source: Stubb in an interview with German tabloid Bild
Quote: "Today, Ukraine is in a stronger and better position than at any other point during this war – militarily, politically and financially.
Ukraine has the upper hand, and it will win this war."
Details: In Stubb's view, "if you survive, if you remain independent, if you remain a sovereign state – that is a victory".
For the president, supporting Ukraine is also an investment in their own security.
Quote: "We must understand – you in Germany and we in Finland – that Ukraine is the best security guarantee we have against Russia. If Ukraine loses, we lose."
Details: Stubb also expressed doubts about the possibility of a Russian nuclear strike against Ukraine, saying that this summer "the Chinese foreign minister visited me, and I raised this issue. And he said: 'We will never allow that to happen.' And I believe that's a fairly effective deterrent."
Background:
- Stubb said he does not seek to be a public participant in negotiations on ending the Russia-Ukraine war, but is ready to become a negotiator if necessary.
- He also said Ukraine needs to be prepared for the "worst" scenario regarding the situation this winter.

articles.title: Israeli strike kills two people including a 3-year-old boy, Gaza medics say
articles.body:
Israeli strike kills two people including a 3-year-old boy, Gaza medics say
CAIRO, Aug 30 - An Israeli airstrike killed two Palestinians, including a three-year-old child, in the central Gaza Strip on Sunday, health officials said.
Gaza medics said the Israeli airstrike near a bakery in Deir Al-Balah killed one man, Hussam Nusair, a three-year-old boy, Tayyem Hamdan, and wounded several others.
The Israeli military said it attacked and killed a Hamas militant. It said that Nusair advanced attacks against Israeli forces and civilians.
Hamas did not immediately comment on the military's allegation.
An October 2025 U.S.-backed ceasefire halted major fighting in the shattered territory, but it failed to end strikes by the Israeli military, which it said aimed to thwart attacks by Hamas and other Gaza militants.
Hamas accuses Israel of violating the ceasefire and undermining efforts to implement a broader plan by U.S. President Donald Trump to end the Gaza conflict, which also includes Israeli withdrawals and Hamas disarmament.
More than 1,300 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire took effect last October, according to Gazan health officials, while the Israeli military says four Israeli soldiers have been killed. REUTERS

articles.title: Iranian officials rally behind Leader's directive for unity and resistance
articles.body:
Iranian officials rally behind Leader's directive for unity and resistance
TEHRAN — Iran’s executive, legislative, judicial, and national security leadership have responded with unified endorsement following the major strategic address delivered by the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei.
In a series of coordinated statements, top officials across all branches of governance described the Leader’s annual Government Week message as an indispensable, comprehensive blueprint for defending national sovereignty, countering hostile economic blockades, and safeguarding domestic social cohesion.
Leading the domestic response, the administration of President Masoud Pezeshkian issued a formal statement on Saturday expressing its profound appreciation for the "wise guidance" of Ayatollah Khamenei. The cabinet noted that the Leader’s words have brought "joy, encouragement and hope" to officials serving the Iranian public during a period of complex national challenges.
Describing the Leader's confidence and support as "the greatest asset and source of support," the administration affirmed that while it fully recognizes the economic pressures stemming from foreign sanctions and recent imposed wars, its immediate priority remains addressing interconnected economic challenges. The government outlined plans to focus on controlling inflation, managing domestic markets, generating employment, directing investment toward domestic production, and steadily reducing reliance on the US dollar.
"We commit ourselves to ensuring prosperity and improving the livelihoods of our dear people in a manner worthy of their dignity," the cabinet statement read, reiterating its full adherence to resistance-economy principles and reliance on internal capabilities.
The administration also identified the preservation of national unity as an absolute priority. In direct response to the Leader’s directive against divisive political conduct, the executive branch confirmed that every major political, economic, social, and cultural decision going forward will incorporate a mandatory "national cohesion component."
"We consider avoiding artificial polarization and discouraging statements to be our definite duty," the statement added, pledging to devote all state efforts toward strengthening consensus, solidarity, and hope across Iranian society. On foreign policy, the administration emphasized that Iranian diplomacy will continue to operate on the guiding principles of "dignity, wisdom, and prudence," promising to firmly resist foreign sanctions and the "unjust schemes of US-Israeli arrogance" through heightened coordination between diplomatic and defense sectors.
Echoing the executive branch, Judiciary Chief Gholam-Hossein Mohseni Eje’i described the Leader’s message as a roadmap for all government officials and servants of the state. He emphasized that strict adherence to the Leader’s guidance represents the only viable path to successfully overcoming current historical challenges.
“The Leader’s enlightening message is a roadmap for all officials and servants of the system and the people,” Mohseni Eje’i stated, underscoring the critical importance of strengthening national unity and rejecting any discourse that could cultivate division. “We reject any form of discord and division in this challenging and eventful path.” He added that from a revolutionary perspective, the unbreakable bond between the Iranian public and the leadership constitutes an “impenetrable barrier” against enemy hybrid warfare.
In the legislative realm, Parliament Speaker Mohammad-Baqer Qalibaf similarly declared that the Leader’s message must serve as the primary guiding principle for all state authorities. Writing in a post on X, Qalibaf emphasized that avoiding actions that could damage social solidarity is both a strategic and moral mandate. “Any action that harms social cohesion is, for all of us, both a national and religious prohibition,” Qalibaf stated. “We pledge to the people and the Leader that, to the very end, we will devote ourselves to serving the people and advancing Iran.”
Concurrently, Iran’s top security official, Mohsen Rezaei, affirmed that the Leader’s remarks “constitute a clear and unequivocal strategy for everyone.” Rezaei stressed that in the current geopolitical environment, “national unity and social cohesion are among the most fundamental components of national power and security.”
The unanimous alignment among senior Iranian leadership follows the address delivered on Friday by Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei to mark Government Week—an annual period held to commemorate President Mohammad Ali Rajai and Prime Minister Mohammad Javad Bahonar, who were assassinated in the bombing of the prime minister’s office on August 30, 1981.
In his message, the Leader honored the memory of the martyred presidents Rajai and Ebrahim Raeisi, the martyred prime minister Bahonar, and all martyred employees, managers, and ministers of various administrations. He paid special tribute to "the great martyr Leader Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei, who held the office of president for nearly two terms."
Ayatollah Khamenei expressed his deep appreciation for the active employees and managers of government institutions, offering specific praise for "the sincere and caring" President Pezeshkian.
“In particular, I commend the worthy measures they have taken, despite the various restrictions and plots of the American-Zionist enemy, and the intensification of sanctions and blockades, during the third imposed war and afterward, to ensure the provision of goods and various services needed by the people, repair key damaged areas, and manage energy,” the Leader stated.
He stressed that the nation of Iran, having “demonstrated its true mettle” over the past six months amid US-Israeli aggression, is fully entitled to feel the concrete services rendered by the various branches of the administration.
Turning to economic governance, Ayatollah Khamenei addressed a chain of livelihood challenges, including inflation, emphasizing the need to focus on core economic pillars. He explicitly called for “boosting production, gradually phasing out the dollar from its important role, and ultimately placing the entire set of resistance-economy policies at the center.”
“The key to resolving all these matters in this field lies in relying as much as possible on domestic production,” the Leader stressed, noting that where domestic capacity is insufficient, imports must be managed "properly and wisely."
These remarks come at a time when the United States has launched a broad initiative titled “Operation Economic Outcast,” following Washington's failure to achieve its broader war objectives against Iran. Addressing these external pressures, the Leader noted that while enemy conduct during and after the war is not without effect, "ever-smarter management of the components of this field, seeking the assistance of the people and experts, and bringing new capacities into operation will guide the country toward the expansion of affairs and development."
Warning against falling into foreign psychological traps, Ayatollah Khamenei highlighted: “The sworn enemy of this nation tries to convey that the path to development and progress lies in following it and complying with its unreasonable demands; whereas observing what it has done to this country and its resources in past periods, even years before the Islamic Revolution, shows otherwise.”
As a key driver for future growth, the Leader urged the “application of technologies and innovations proposed by young elites.” He observed that making timely use of these technological advantages and stepping away from routine procedures and established habits can trigger effective leaps in the country’s overall advancement.

articles.title: IRGC claims to have thwarted Israeli, US-linked terror cell in southeastern Iran
articles.body:
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on Saturday announced that security forces thwarted the activities of a "terrorist cell" that it claimed was linked to Israel and the United States and operated in Sistan and Baluchistan Province in southeastern Iran.
According to the IRGC statement, one member of the cell was killed and six other suspects, including members and supporters of the group, were arrested.
In a statement issued by the public relations office of the Quds Base of the IRGC Ground Forces, it was claimed that the cell was located shortly after its members entered the area and that they intended to carry out acts of sabotage and attacks against preselected targets in the southern part of the province.
The operation against the cell was carried out jointly by the IRGC, Iran’s Intelligence Ministry, and the Sistan and Baluchistan provincial police. According to Iranian authorities, the identification of the group’s members was made possible through prolonged intelligence monitoring.
During the operation, one suspect was killed, and six others were arrested before they were able, according to Tehran, to carry out their planned activities.
Iran claims to have found explosives, Starlink communication equipment
Iranian security forces claimed that during searches, they seized 20 packages containing explosives and equipment related to the preparation of explosive devices. They also said they found small and medium caliber weapons, a large quantity of ammunition, and communications equipment based on the Starlink satellite system.
The IRGC statement claimed that the group was connected to the “Israeli regime” and the “American terrorist regime,” according to the wording of the Iranian announcement. It further claimed that the cell members planned to carry out a series of attacks in the province as part of an operation coordinated with the United States, but were arrested before they could execute their plans.
The IRGC warned individuals it claimed were operating on behalf of Israel and the United States against attempting further activity in the region. The statement said that the security of Sistan and Baluchistan residents constitutes a “red line,” and that Iranian security forces would not allow hostile elements to enter the province or operate there.
The claims regarding Israeli and American involvement are based on the IRGC statement, and no independent evidence verifying them was presented in the report.

articles.title: Drones attack Russia’s Leningrad region and Bryansk overnight
articles.body:
Drones attack Russia’s Leningrad region and Bryansk overnight
According to Ukrinform, this information was reported by the ASTRA Telegram channel.
On the night of August 30, residents of the Leningrad Region released footage showing the repulsion of a drone attack and a large-scale fire at what is believed to be the “Kirishinefteorgsintez” oil refinery.
In the morning, Leningrad Oblast Governor Oleksandr Drozdhenko reported that a fire had broken out in the industrial zone of the city of Kirishi as a result of strikes by Ukrainian drones. No official reports of casualties have been released.
An ASTRA OSINT analyst determined that the building that was hit is located in the Leningrad Oblast, in the city of Kirishi.
In addition, during a UAV attack in Bryansk, an explosion occurred near apartment buildings in the Bezhitsky District.
The Bryansk Electromechanical Plant (BEMZ) and the Bryansk Automobile Plant (BAZ) (part of the Almaz-Antey Aerospace Defense Concern) are located 4–5 kilometers from the site of the explosion.
BEMZ manufactures electronics for the Russian Armed Forces. Its main and best-known product is the “Krasukha” radar and communications jamming systems. The plant also assembles radio monitoring and radio-technical reconnaissance stations, ground-based electronic warfare (EW) systems, satellite data reception and processing systems, as well as individual components and parts for airborne radar systems and aircraft radars.
As reported by Ukrinform, on the night of Friday, August 22, following a drone attack in Russia, fires broke out at an Ozon warehouse, an oil refinery, and the seaport of Yeysk.
